Listing Memorandum




                               US$220,000,000 8.500% Senior Secured Notes due 2032
We are offering US$220,000,000 aggregate principal amount of 8.500% senior secured notes due 2032. The notes will mature on October 28, 2032.
Interest will accrue from April 28, 2026, and will be payable semi-annually, in arrears on April 28 and October 28 of each year, commencing on October
28, 2026.
The notes are issued as additional notes (the “Additional Notes”) pursuant to the indenture dated as of October 29, 2025, pursuant to which we previously
issued US$750,000,000 aggregate principal amount of 8.500% senior secured notes due 2032 (the “Initial Notes” and, together with the Additional Notes
offered hereby, the “Notes”). The Additional Notes have the same terms in all respects as the Initial Notes (except with respect to the date of issuance and
the initial issuance price), are treated as part of the same series of securities as the Initial Notes under the indenture and will become fully fungible with the
Initial Notes following the termination of the 40-day distribution compliance period commencing on the New Issue Date (as defined below). Holders of the
Additional Notes and the Initial Notes vote as one class under the indenture. See “Listing and General Information.”
The Notes will be guaranteed on a senior basis by the subsidiary guarantors described in “Description of Notes” (the “Subsidiary Guarantors”) and secured
by first priority liens on the Collateral (as defined in “Description of Notes”). The Notes will rank equal in right of payment with all other existing and
future senior indebtedness of the Company, and the guarantees will rank equal in right of payment with all other existing and future indebtedness of the
Subsidiary Guarantors. See “Description of Notes—General.” The Notes and the guarantees will be senior obligations of the Company and the Subsidiary
Guarantors, respectively, secured by first priority liens on the Collateral (as defined herein), subject to permitted liens and certain other exceptions as
described under “Description of Notes—Collateral.” The Notes and the guarantees will be effectively (i) pari passu with all existing and future
indebtedness permitted to be secured by a first-priority lien on the Collateral, subject to permitted collateral liens and existing liens and rights on the
Collateral, (ii) senior in right of payment to all existing and future subordinated indebtedness of the Company and the Subsidiary Guarantors, and (iii) senior
to all other existing and future senior indebtedness of the Company and the Subsidiary Guarantors that is unsecured or that is secured by junior liens or liens
that are not on the Collateral, in each case to the extent of the value of the Collateral. The Notes and the guarantees will be effectively subordinated to (i)
the extent of the value of the collateral securing (x) all existing and future secured indebtedness of the Company to the extent such security interest does not
also secure the Notes, and (y) all existing and future secured indebtedness of the Subsidiary Guarantors to the extent such security interest does not also
secure the guarantees, (ii) all additional existing and future indebtedness of the Company’s subsidiaries that does not provide a guarantee, and (iii)
obligations of the Company or the Subsidiary Guarantors preferred by statute or by operation of law.
We may redeem the Notes in whole or in part at any time on or after October 28, 2028 at a redemption price specified in this offering memorandum, plus
accrued and unpaid interest, if any, to the date of redemption. Before October 28, 2028, we may redeem some or all of the Notes at a redemption price equal
to 100% of the principal amount of the Notes redeemed plus a “make-whole” premium, plus accrued and unpaid interest, in any, to the date of redemption.
Upon the occurrence of specified events relating to tax law as a result of which we will be obligated to pay additional interest amounts with respect to the
Notes, the Notes will be redeemable at a price equal to 100% of the principal amount of the Notes, plus accrued and unpaid interest, if any, to the date of
redemption. We may also redeem up to 35% of the aggregate principal amount of the Notes using the proceeds of certain equity offerings completed on or
before October 28, 2028 at the redemption price set out in this offering memorandum, plus accrued and unpaid interest, if any, to the date of redemption. If
we experience specific kinds of changes in control, or, subject to certain conditions, we sell certain of our assets, we must offer to purchase the Notes. See
“Risk Factors” beginning on page 15 for a discussion of certain risks that you should consider in connection with an investment in the Notes.
The Notes have not been registered under the Securities Act of 1933, as amended (the “Securities Act”), or the securities laws of any jurisdiction.
We are offering the Notes only to qualified institutional buyers under Rule 144A under the Securities Act and non-U.S. persons outside the United
States in reliance on Regulation S of the Securities Act. For a description of certain restrictions on transfer of the Notes, see “Transfer
Restrictions.” In addition, during the 40-day period following the issue date, the Notes offered pursuant to Regulation S will be subject to certain
U.S. selling restrictions, and, therefore, will have temporary CUSIPs and ISINs during that period.
Application has been made to list the Additional Notes on the Official List of the Luxembourg Stock Exchange and to admit the Additional Notes to trading
on the Euro MTF Market of the Luxembourg Stock Exchange. Our LEI code is 549300XKJ91C4SZLG750. This offering memorandum constitutes a
prospectus for the purposes of the Luxembourg law on prospectuses for securities, dated July 16, 2019.
None of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, any U.S. state securities commission or any securities regulatory authority has approved or
disapproved of these securities or determined whether this offering memorandum is accurate or complete. Any representation to the contrary is a criminal
offense.
The Notes and the information contained in this offering memorandum have not been, and will not be, registered with or approved by the Peruvian
Superintendency of the Securities Market (Superintendencia del Mercado de Valores, or “SMV”) or the Lima Stock Exchange (Bolsa de Valores de Lima,
or the “BVL”). Accordingly, the Notes cannot be offered or sold in the Republic of Peru (“Peru”), except if such offering is considered a private offering
under the securities laws and regulations of Peru. The Peruvian Securities Market Law, approved by Legislative Decree No. 861, whose sole text was
enacted by Supreme Decree No. 020-2023-EF, as amended (the “Peruvian Securities Market Law”), establishes, among other things, that any particular
offer may qualify as private if it is directed exclusively to institutional investors. The Notes may not be offered or sold in Peru or in any other jurisdiction
except in compliance with the securities laws thereof.

Issue price per Additional Note: 102.705% plus accrued interest, from (and including) April 28, 2026
to, but excluding the New Issue Date (as defined below) totaling U.S.$13.22 per $1,000 principal amount of Additional Notes
                 plus additional interest, if any, from the New Issue Date, if settlement occurs after that date.

Delivery of the Notes was made to investors in book-entry form through The Depository Trust Company (“DTC”) for the accounts of its direct and indirect
participants, including Euroclear Bank S.A.N.V., as operator of the Euroclear System (“Euroclear”), and Clearstream Banking, société anonyme
(“Clearstream”), on June 24, 2026 (the “New Issue Date”).
                                                                 Global Coordinators
                                BofA Securities                      BTG Pactual                 Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC
                                                                 Joint Book-Runners
                                                      BBVA                                Natixis


                                                                      July 8, 2026

Unless otherwise indicated or the context otherwise requires, all references in this offering memorandum to
“Volcan,” the “issuer,” “Company,” “we,” “us” and words of similar effect refer to Volcan Compañía Minera
S.A.A. with its consolidated subsidiaries unless the context otherwise requires. Unless otherwise specified or the
context otherwise requires, in this offering memorandum a reference to a law or a provision of a law is a reference to
that law or provision as extended, amended or re-enacted.

          For the sale of the Notes in the United States, we are relying upon an exemption from registration under the
Securities Act for an offer and sale of securities that does not involve a public offering. By purchasing the Notes,
you will be deemed to have made certain acknowledgments, representations and agreements as set forth under
“Transfer Restrictions.” We are not, and the initial purchasers are not, making an offer to sell the Notes in any
jurisdiction except where such an offer or sale is permitted. You should understand that you will be required to bear
the financial risks of your investment for an indefinite period of time.

          We have submitted this offering memorandum solely to a limited number of qualified institutional buyers
and to persons other than U.S. persons so they can consider a purchase of the Notes. We have not authorized the use
of this offering memorandum for any other purpose. By accepting delivery of this offering memorandum, you agree
to these restrictions. See “Transfer Restrictions.”

          The market information in this offering memorandum has been obtained from publicly available sources
deemed by us to be reliable. Such information has been accurately reproduced and as far as we are aware and are
able to ascertain from information published by such sources, no facts have been omitted which would render the
reproduced information inaccurate or misleading. We and the initial purchasers cannot assure you that such
information provided to us is accurate or complete. This offering memorandum summarizes certain documents and
other information, and we refer you to them for a more complete understanding of what we discuss in this offering
memorandum. In making an investment decision, you must rely solely on your own examination of us and the terms
of the offering and the Notes, including the merits and risks involved.

         We are not making any representation to any purchaser regarding the legality of an investment in the Notes
by such purchaser under any legal investment or similar laws or regulations. You should not consider any
information in this offering memorandum to be legal, business, tax or other advice or recommendation with respect
to any investment. You should consult your own counsel, accountant, business advisor and tax advisor for legal,
tax, business and financial advice regarding any investment in the Notes.

         We are responsible for the information contained in this offering memorandum. We confirm that, after
having made all reasonable inquiries, this offering memorandum contains all information with regard to us and the
Notes that is material to the offering and sale of the Notes, that the information contained in this offering
memorandum is true and accurate in all material respects and is not misleading and that there are no omissions of
any facts from this offering memorandum which, by their absence herefrom, make this offering memorandum
misleading. We have not, and the initial purchasers have not, authorized any person to provide you with different
information or to make any representation not contained in this offering memorandum. You should assume that the
information contained in this offering memorandum is accurate only as of the date on the front cover of this offering
memorandum. Our business, financial condition, results of operations and prospects may have changed since that
date.

         By purchasing any of our Notes, you will be deemed to have acknowledged that: (1) you have received a
copy and have reviewed this offering memorandum; (2) you have had an opportunity to review all financial and
other information considered by you to be necessary to make your investment decision and to verify the accuracy of,
or to supplement, the information contained in this offering memorandum and have been offered the opportunity to
ask us questions, and received answers, as you deemed necessary in connection with your investment decision;
(3) you have not relied on the initial purchasers or any person affiliated with the initial purchasers in connection with
your investigation of the accuracy of such information or your investment decision; (4) the initial purchasers are not
responsible for, and are not making any representation to you concerning us, our future performance or the accuracy
or completeness of this offering memorandum and they take no responsibility with respect to the information
contained herein; and (5) no person has been authorized to give any information or to make any representation
concerning us or the Notes or the offer and sale of the Notes, other than as contained in this offering memorandum.

You should contact the initial purchasers with any questions about this offering or if you require additional
information to verify the information contained in this offering memorandum.

         We reserve the right to withdraw this offering of the Notes at any time, and we and the initial purchasers
reserve the right to reject any commitment to subscribe for the Notes in whole or in part and to allot to any
prospective investor less than the full amount of Notes sought by that investor. The initial purchasers and certain
related entities may acquire for their own account a portion of the Notes.

         You must comply with all applicable laws and regulations in force in any jurisdiction in connection with
the possession or distribution of this offering memorandum and the purchase, offer or sale of the Notes and you
must obtain any consent, approval or permission required by you for the purchase, offer or sale of the Notes under
the laws and regulations applicable to you in force in any jurisdiction to which you are subject or in which you make
such purchase, offer or sale, and neither we nor the initial purchasers will have any responsibility therefor.

          The distribution of this offering memorandum and the offering and sale of the Notes in certain jurisdictions
may be restricted by law. We and the initial purchasers require persons in possession of this offering memorandum
to inform themselves about and to observe any such restrictions. This offering memorandum does not constitute an
offer of, or an invitation to purchase, any of the Notes in any jurisdiction in which such offer or invitation would be
unlawful.

         The contents of our website do not form part of this offering memorandum.

                                       NOTICE TO CERTAIN INVESTORS

Notice to Investors within the United Kingdom

     The Notes are not intended to be offered, sold, distributed or otherwise made available to and should not be
offered, sold, distributed or otherwise made available to any retail investor in the United Kingdom (“UK”). For these
purposes, a retail investor means a person who is either one (or both) of the following: (i) not a professional client, as
defined in point (8) of Article 2(1) of Regulation (EU) No 600/2014 as it forms part of domestic law by virtue of the
European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 (“EUWA”) ("UK MiFIR"); or (ii) not a qualified investor as defined in
paragraph 15 of Schedule 1 to the Public Offers and Admissions to Trading Regulations 2024 (the "POATRs").
Consequently no disclosure document required by the FCA Product Disclosure Sourcebook (“DISC”), for offering,
selling or distributing the Notes or otherwise making them available to retail investors in the UK has been prepared
and therefore offering, selling or distributing the Notes or otherwise making them available to any retail investor in
the UK may be unlawful under DISC and the Consumer Composite Investments (Designated Activities) Regulations
2024 (the "CCI Regulations").

Notice to Investors within the European Economic Area

     The Notes are not intended to be offered, sold or otherwise made available to and should not be offered, sold or
otherwise made available to any retail investor in the European Economic Area (“EEA”). For these purposes, a retail
investor means a person who is one (or more) of: (i) a retail client as defined in point (11) of Article 4(1) of Directive
2014/65/EU (as amended, “MiFID II”); or (ii) a customer within the meaning of Directive (EU) 2016/97 (as amended,
the “Insurance Distribution Directive”), where that customer would not qualify as a professional client as defined in
point (10) of Article 4(1) of MiFID II; or (iii) not a qualified investor as defined in Regulation (EU) 2017/1129 (as
amended, the “Prospectus Regulation”). Consequently no key information document required by Regulation (EU)
No 1286/2014 (as amended, the “PRIIPs Regulation”) for offering or selling the Notes or otherwise making them
available to retail investors in the EEA has been prepared and therefore offering or selling the Notes or otherwise
making them available to any retail investor in the EEA may be unlawful under the PRIIPs Regulation.



                                          ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

        We have agreed that while any Notes remain outstanding and are “restricted securities” as defined in
Rule 144(a)(3) under the Securities Act, we will make available, upon request, to any holder or prospective

purchaser of Notes the information required pursuant to Rule 144A(d)(4) under the Securities Act with respect to us
during any period in which we are not subject to Section 13 or 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as
amended (the “Exchange Act”) or exempt by virtue of Rule 12g3 2(b) thereunder. Any such request should be
directed to us at our principal office at Av. Manuel Olguín 373, Santiago de Surco, Lima, Peru.

         We are a publicly held corporation (sociedad anónima abierta) incorporated in Peru. Our Class A voting
shares and our Class B non-voting shares are registered with the Public Registry of the Securities Market (Registro
Público del Mercado de Valores) of the SMV and listed on the Lima Stock Exchange (Bolsa de Valores de Lima).
Accordingly, we are currently required to file certain information in Spanish with the SMV and the Lima Stock
Exchange such as quarterly and annual reports and notices of material events (hechos de importancia). All such
reports and notices are available at www.smv.gob.pe and www.bvl.com.pe. The documents filed with the SMV and
the Lima Stock Exchange are not a part of this offering memorandum and are not incorporated by reference herein.

                                       ENFORCEMENT OF JUDGMENTS

          We are incorporated as a publicly held corporation (sociedad anónima abierta) under the laws of Peru.
Substantially all of our directors and officers, as well as certain of the experts named herein, reside in Peru or
elsewhere outside the United States and a substantial portion of their assets may be, and substantially all of our
assets are, located in Peru or elsewhere outside the United States. As a result, it may not be possible for investors to
effect service of process within the United States or elsewhere outside Peru upon us or upon any of our directors or
officers or to enforce against such parties in courts outside Peru judgments predicated solely upon the civil liability
provisions of the federal securities laws of the United States or other foreign regulations. In addition, there may be
doubt as to whether the courts of Peru would enforce in all respects, to the same extent and in as timely a manner as
a U.S. court or foreign court, an action predicated solely upon the civil liability provisions of the U.S. federal
securities laws or other foreign regulations.

          We have been advised by Payet, Rey, Cauvi, Pérez Abogados, our Peruvian counsel, that any final and
conclusive judgment for a fixed and definitive sum obtained against us and/or any of the Subsidiary Guarantors in
any foreign court having jurisdiction in respect of any suit, action or proceeding against us and/or any of the
Subsidiary Guarantors for the enforcement of any of the obligations assumed under this offering memorandum or
the Notes would, upon request, be deemed valid and enforceable in Peru through an exequatur judiciary proceeding
(which does not involve the reopening of the case or reexamination of the merits of the case), provided that:
(a) there is in effect a treaty between the country where said foreign court sits and Peru regarding the recognition
and enforcement of foreign judgments; or (b) in the absence of such a treaty, the original judgment is ratified by the
Peruvian courts (Cortes de la República del Perú), provided that the following conditions and requirements are met:

         (i)      the foreign judgment does not resolve matters under the exclusive jurisdiction of
         Peruvian courts (and the matters contemplated by this offering memorandum or the Notes are not
         matters under the exclusive jurisdiction of Peruvian courts);

         (ii)     the relevant foreign court had jurisdiction under its own conflicts of law rules and under
         general principles of international procedural jurisdiction;

         (iii)    the defendant was served in accordance with the laws of the place where such proceeding
         took place, was granted a reasonable opportunity to appear before such foreign court, and was
         guaranteed due process rights;

         (iv)     the foreign judgment has the status of res judicata in the jurisdiction of the court
         rendering such judgment;

         (v)      there is no pending litigation in Peru between the same parties for the same dispute,
         which shall have been initiated before the commencement of the proceeding that concluded with
         the foreign judgment;

         (vi)    the foreign judgment is not incompatible with another judgment that fulfills the
         requirements of recognition and enforceability established by Peruvian law unless such foreign
         judgment was rendered first;

(vii)   the foreign judgment is not contrary to public policy (orden público) or good morals
         (buenas costumbres) of Peru;

         (viii)  it is not proven that the foreign court that rendered the foreign judgment denies
         enforcement of Peruvian judgments or engages in a review of the merits thereof;

         (ix)      a copy of such judgment has been (a) in case of jurisdictions that are party to the 1961
         Hague Convention Abolishing the Requirements of Legalization of Foreign Public Documents
         (“The Hague Apostille Convention”), duly apostilled by the competent authority of the jurisdiction
         of the issuing court, or (b) in case of jurisdictions that are not party to The Hague Apostille
         Convention, certified by Peruvian consular authorities and, in each case, is accompanied by a
         certified and officially translated copy of such judgment into Spanish by a Peruvian Certified
         translator; and

         (x)      the applicable court taxes or fees have been paid.

         We have no reason to believe that any of our obligations relating to the Notes would be contrary to
Peruvian public policy (orden público), good morals (buenas costumbres) and international treaties binding upon
Peru or generally accepted principles of international law.

         Some of our properties could be subject to the exemption set forth under Article No. 616 of the Peruvian
Civil Procedure Code (Legislative Decree No. 768, whose sole unified text was approved through Ministerial
Resolution No. 010-93-JUS) pursuant to which the property of any private entity assigned to render essential public
services may not be subject to preliminary attachments (medida cautelar) that could affect the normal rendering of
such services.

          In the past, Peruvian courts have enforced judgments rendered in the United States based on legal
principles of reciprocity and comity. However, the United States does not currently have a treaty with Peru
providing for reciprocal recognition and enforcement of judgments in civil and commercial matters. Therefore,
unless the above-mentioned requirements are satisfied, a final judgment for payment of money rendered by a federal
or state court in the United States based on civil liability, whether or not predicated solely upon U.S. federal
securities laws, may not be enforceable, either in whole or in part, in Peru. However, if the party in whose favor
such unenforced final judgment was rendered brings a new suit in a competent court in Peru, such party may submit
to the Peruvian court the final judgment rendered in the United States. Under such circumstances, a judgment by a
federal or state court of the United States against us and/or of the Subsidiary Guarantors may be regarded by a
Peruvian court only as evidence of the outcome of the dispute to which such judgment relates, and a Peruvian court
may choose to re-hear the dispute. In addition, awards of punitive damages in actions brought in the United States or
elsewhere are unenforceable in Peru.

           CAUTIONARY STATEMENT REGARDING FORWARD-LOOKING STATEMENTS

         This offering memorandum contains certain forward-looking statements within the meaning of Section 21E
of the Exchange Act, and Section 27A of the Securities Act. Statements that do not relate strictly to historical or
current facts are forward-looking and usually identified by the use of words such as “anticipate,” “estimate,”
“forecasts,” “approximate,” “expect,” “project,” “intend,” “plan,” “believe,” “will,” “may” and other words of
similar meaning in connection with any discussion of future operating or financial matters. Such statements are
made in reliance upon the safe harbor provisions of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995.

         Without limiting the generality of the foregoing, forward-looking statements in this offering memorandum
include statements regarding expected commencement dates of mining or metal production operations, projected
quantities of future metal production, anticipated production rates, operating efficiencies, costs and expenditures,
including taxes, as well as projected demand or supply for our products. Actual results could differ materially
depending upon factors including the risks and uncertainties relating to general Peruvian and international economic
and political conditions, the cyclical and volatile prices of the metals we produce, other commodities and supplies,
including fuel and electricity, availability of materials, insurance coverage, equipment, required permits or approvals
and financing, the occurrence of unusual weather or operating conditions, epidemics and pandemics and other health
outbreaks, cyber-attacks and system integrity, lower than expected ore grades, water and geological problems, the

failure of equipment or processes to operate in accordance with specifications, failure to obtain financial assurance
to meet closure and remediation obligations, labor relations, litigation and environmental risks, as well as political
and economic risk associated with our operations. Results of operations are directly affected by metals prices, which
can be volatile. These statements involve risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially
from projected results. Accordingly, investors should not place undue reliance on forward-looking statements as a
prediction of actual results. We have based these forward-looking statements on current expectations and
assumptions about future events. While we consider these expectations and assumptions to be reasonable, they are
inherently subject to significant business, economic, competitive, regulatory and other risks and uncertainties, most
of which are difficult to predict and many of which are beyond our control. The risks and uncertainties that may
affect our operations, performance and results and the forward-looking statements include, but are not limited to,
those set forth under “Risk Factors.”

                              PRESENTATION OF FINANCIAL INFORMATION

Currencies and Exchange Rates

         Unless otherwise specified herein or the context otherwise requires, in this offering memorandum
references to “Peru” are to the Republic of Peru; references to the “Peruvian government” are to the government of
the Republic of Peru; references to the “United States” or the “U.S.” are to the United States of America; references
to “US$” and “U.S. dollars” are to United States dollars, and references to “S/” and “soles” are to Peruvian soles.

        Unless otherwise indicated, translations of sol amounts into U.S. dollars in this offering memorandum have
been made at the period-end rates of each corresponding period. For a complete description of the exchange rates
between the sol and the U.S. dollar, see “Exchange Rates.” The Federal Reserve Bank of New York does not report
a noon buying rate for soles.

Financial Statements

         Our audited consolidated financial statements included in this offering memorandum fairly represent our
financial position as of December 31, 2024 and 2025 and our results of operations for each of the two years ended
December 31, 2024 and 2025. Our unaudited interim condensed consolidated financial statements included in this
offering memorandum fairly represent our financial position as of March 31, 2026 and our results of operations for
the three months ended March 31, 2025 and 2026.

         Our consolidated financial statements as of and for the year ended December 31, 2025 have been audited
by Gaveglio Aparicio y Asociados Sociedad Civil de Responsabilidad Limitada, a member firm of the
PricewaterhouseCoopers International Limited network, and our interim condensed consolidated financial
statements as of March 31, 2026 and for the three months ended March 31, 2026 have been subject to the limited
review of Gaveglio Aparicio y Asociados Sociedad Civil de Responsabilidad Limitada, a member firm of the
PricewaterhouseCoopers International Limited network. Our consolidated financial statements as of and for the year
ended December 31, 2024 have been audited by Velásquez, Loli y Asociados S. Civil de R.L., affiliate of a member
firm of Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu Limited.

        The comparative values as of December 31, 2024 in the financial statements included in this offering
memorandum have been reissued and reclassified from those originally published to correct certain misstatements
that management has determined are not material, both individually and in the aggregate, to the Company’s
consolidated financial statements. The correcting adjustments include the reclassification of:

         (i)       US$74.1 million of proceeds from the sale of shares of energy companies from net cash
         used in financing activities to net cash used in investing activities on the consolidated statement of
         cash flows;

         (ii)   US$5.0 million of real estate assets incorrectly reported within property, plant and
         equipment on the consolidated balance sheet to investment properties;

         (iii)    US$10.5 million incorrectly reported as legal reserve to retained earnings; and

(iv)     US$1.0 million of certain payments to suppliers related to leases from net cash used in
         operating activities to net cash used in financing activities on the consolidated statement of cash
         flows.

         The aggregate impact of the misstatements resulted in an overstatement of previously reported net cash
flows provided by operating activities of US$1.0 million, the overstatement of previously reported net cash flows
used in investing activities of US$74.1 million and the understatement of previously reported net cash flows used in
financing activities of US$75.2 million. No other totals or subtotals in any of the consolidated financial statements
were affected by the misstatements.

          In addition to the above, the Company applied other immaterial voluntary reclassifications to (i) certain line
items within current assets and current liabilities reported in the consolidated balance sheet, (ii) current and non-
current lease liabilities reported within the financial obligations in the consolidated balance sheet and (iii) certain
items reported within net cash used in financing activities reported in the consolidated statement of cash flows. Such
reclassifications were not made to correct previously reported misstatements and do not affect any totals or subtotals
contained in any of the financial statements.

Special Note Regarding Non-IFRS Financial Measures

         We prepare our financial statements in U.S. dollars and in conformity with IFRS Accounting Standards, as
issued by the International Accounting Standards Board (“IASB”) (“IFRS”) and, in respect of our unaudited interim
condensed consolidated financial statements as of March 31, 2026 and for the three months ended March 31, 2025
and 2026, in accordance with International Accounting Standard (“IAS”) 34 “Interim Financial Reporting,” the
standard of IFRS applicable to the preparation of interim financial statements.

          This offering memorandum presents several non-IFRS measures, including EBITDA, Adjusted EBITDA,
net financial debt and unit cost. EBITDA is calculated as net (loss) profit for the year/period before income tax
expense, financial expenses (income), depreciation and amortization during such period. Adjusted EBITDA is
calculated by eliminating from the calculation of EBITDA: (a) any non-recurring items during such period, (b) gains
or losses on the sale of property (other than the sale of property in the ordinary course of business) during such
period, (c) any other non-cash items deducted from or included in the calculation of pre-tax net income for such
period (other than items that will require cash payments and for which an accrual or reserve has been, or is required
by IFRS to be, made), and (d) foreign exchange gains or losses upon loans and foreign currency translation
adjustments or monetary correction and bank charges. Net financial debt is calculated as current and non-current
borrowings minus operating leases (IFRS 16), bank overdrafts, and cash and cash equivalents. Unit cost is reported
on a quarterly basis and is calculated by dividing the total production cost by the tonnage treated, expressing the cost
incurred per unit of material processed, including all direct costs of mining such as costs associated with extraction,
leaching and further processing of metal ores, as well as labor, transportation and physical plant costs associated
with those processes. Unit cost figures are given as nominal dollar amounts, usually expressed as dollars per metric
tonne, and exclude provisions, amortization, depreciation and central office costs and purchases of concentrates.

          EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA are presented for the convenience of investors because we deem them to
better represent our operating and economic performance. We believe that EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA, while
providing useful information, should not be considered in isolation or as a substitute for net income, as an indicator
of operating performance, or as an alternative to cash flow as a measure of liquidity. EBITDA and Adjusted
EBITDA are not IFRS-based measures of liquidity or performance. Additionally, our calculation of EBITDA and
Adjusted EBITDA may be different from the calculation used by other companies and therefore, comparability may
be affected.

         Net financial debt is presented to provide investors with a clearer picture of our leverage and liquidity
position than traditional GAAP balance sheet line items might convey on their own. We believe that net financial
debt, while providing useful information, should not be considered in isolation or as a substitute for financial debt as
an indicator of leverage, or as an alternative to cash flow as a measure of liquidity.

          Unit cost is presented because it is a widely used measure of costs, although it is not an IFRS-based
measure of cost. We believe that unit cost, while providing useful information, should not be considered in isolation
or as a substitute for costs of sales, costs of selling and administrative expenses, or as an indicator of costs.

This offering memorandum also includes unaudited consolidated financial information for the twelve
months ended March 31, 2026, which is calculated by adding the unaudited results for the relevant measure for the
three months ended March 31, 2026 to the audited results for the relevant measure for the year ended December 31,

                                MINERAL RESOURCE AND RESERVE DATA

          In this offering memorandum, we present our holdings in, or rights to, mineral deposits in two categories:
(i) resources and (ii) reserves, as is standard in the industry. Our ore reserve and mineral resource estimates are
consistent with the application of internationally used classifications. The information on reserves and resources
included in this offering memorandum has been estimated following the intent of international definitions as
established by the Joint Ore Reserves Committee Code of Australia (“JORC”) and Canada’s NI 43-101 standard.

         The information on reserves and resources as of December 31, 2025 included in this offering memorandum
has been prepared under the general supervision of our chief geological engineer, and our geology and planning
managers, and was found to be in compliance with those international frameworks by SLR Consulting, a widely
recognized international consulting firm in the mining sector. The report produced by SLR Consulting is not,
however, included in this offering memorandum and is not incorporated by reference into this offering
memorandum, and all information on reverses and resources included herein are prepared by our chief geological
engineer and our geology and planning managers, acting as competent persons.

         Mineral resources are ore bodies of economic value that have been identified and evaluated through
exploration, reconnaissance and sampling. Resources are estimated based on geological knowledge about the
deposit, which is based on scientific concepts concerning the formation of minerals such as oxides, sulfides and
mixed ores, as well as available knowledge concerning the geological continuity of the mineralized sectors. This is

based on technical parameters, such as robustness of the genetic-geological model and its validation through
drillings.

          Resources may be subdivided further, based on the degree of knowledge that we have of their extent and
composition. If our knowledge of the resources is extensive and direct, they are measured resources; if our
knowledge of them is substantial but less extensive, they are indicated resources; and if our knowledge of them is
only indirect, they are inferred resources. Measured resources are based on a dense grid of regularly distributed
drillings, indicated resources are based on an intermediate grid of regularly distributed drillings, and inferred
resources are based on irregularly, sometimes sporadically distributed drillings, where the continuity of ore grades is
mostly supported by concepts on the theoretical continuity of geological events, such as lithology, alteration and
mineralization. Resources that are either measured or indicated, as opposed to inferred, are sometimes together
referred to as demonstrated resources. Resources of all three categories are sometimes referred to, together, as
identified resources.

         A “reserve” is that part of a mineral resource, which, at the time of determination, may be economically
and legally extracted. Reserve estimates are the result of studies that take into account certain technical, economic
and legal factors, which are not considered when estimating mineral resources. Reserve estimates are based on
mineral resource estimates but also reflect beliefs, at the time of determination, regarding the amount of such
resources that can be recovered and sold at prices in excess of the total costs associated with extraction and
processing. Reserve estimates are adjusted as technical, economic and legal circumstances change. Reserves are
typically first determined at the time of planning a full-scale mining project. As a result, reserves are not reported for
certain of our mineral deposits. Reserves may be “proven” or “probable.” Our proven reserves are based on our
measured mineral resources, while our probable reserves are based on our indicated mineral resources, in each case
after undertaking studies regarding certain technical, economic and legal factors.

                                  GLOSSARY OF CERTAIN MINING TERMS

Alteration: Changes in the chemical or mineralogical composition of a rock, generally produced by weathering or
hydrothermal solution.

Assay: The chemical analysis of mineral samples to determine the metal content.

Breccia: A rock composed of broken fragments of minerals or rock cemented together that can be either similar to
or different from the composition of the fragments.

Brownfield exploration: An exploration or development project near or within an existing operation, which can
share infrastructure and management.

Concentration: The process by which crushed and ground ore is separated into metal concentrates and reject
material through processes such as flotation.

Concentrator Plant: A plant where concentration takes place.

Crushing and Grinding: The processes by which ore is broken into small pieces to prepare it for further
processing.

Deposit: A mineralized body that has been physically delineated by sufficient drilling, trenching, and/or
underground work, and found to contain a sufficient average grade of metal or metals to warrant further exploration
and/or development expenditures. Such a deposit does not qualify as a commercially mineable ore body or as
containing reserves or ore, unless final legal, technical and economic factors are resolved.

Development: Activities related to the building of infrastructure and the stripping and opening of mineral deposits,
commencing when economically recoverable reserves can reasonably be estimated to exist and generally continuing
until commercial production begins.

Diamond Drilling: Diamond drilling is used in the mining industry to probe the contents of known ore deposits and
potential sites. By withdrawing a small diameter core of rock from the ore deposit, geologists can analyze the core
by chemical assay and conduct structural and mineralogical studies of the rock.

Exploration: Activities associated with ascertaining the existence, location, extent or quality of a mineral deposit.

Indicated Resources: Resources about which our knowledge is substantial but less extensive than our knowledge of
measured resources.

Inferred Resources: Resources about which our knowledge is only indirect.

Leaching: The process of extracting a soluble metallic compound from an ore by selectively dissolving it in a
suitable solvent.

Leaching plant: A plant where leaching takes place.

LME: London Metal Exchange.

Measured Resources: Resources about which our knowledge is both extensive and direct.

Mill: A machine used to grind ore to the consistency of powder or (in wet grinding) slurry.

Milling: A treatment process in which ore is ground into a fine powder.

Mine: Mines are the source of mineral-bearing material found near the surface or deep in the ground.

Mineral Deposit or Mineralized Material: A mineralized underground body that has been probed by a sufficient
number of closely-spaced drill holes and/or underground sampling measurements to support an estimate of sufficient
tonnage and ore grade to warrant further exploration or development. Mineral deposits or mineralized materials do
not qualify as commercially minable ore reserves (i.e., probable reserves or proven reserves), as prescribed under
standards of the U.S. Bureau of Mines Circular 831 of 1980, until a final and comprehensive economic, technical,
and legal feasibility study based upon the test results has been concluded.

Mineralization: A deposit of rock containing one or more minerals for which the economics of recovery have not
yet been established.

Ore: A mineral or aggregate of minerals from which metal can be economically mined or extracted.

Ore Grade: The average amount of metal expressed as a percentage or in ounces per metric tonne.

Ore Deposit: Category including all resources and reserves.

Ounces: Unit of weight. A troy ounce equals 31,103 grams or 1.097 avoirdupois ounces.

Oxide Ore: Metalliferous minerals altered by weathering, surface waters, and their conversion, partly or wholly,
into oxides, carbonates, or sulfates.

Porphyry: A variety of igneous rock consisting of large-grained crystals, such as feldspar or quartz, dispersed in a
fine-grained groundmass.

Probable Reserves: Reserves about which our knowledge is substantial but less extensive than our knowledge of
Proven Reserves.

Proven Reserves: Reserves about which our knowledge is both extensive and direct. Quantities of Proven Reserves
are computed from dimensions revealed in outcrops, trenches, workings or drill holes, and grade and quality are
computed from the results of detailed sampling. Sites for inspection, sampling and measurement of Proven Reserves
are spaced so closely together, and the geologic character of the ore is so well defined, that its size, shape, depth and
mineral content are well established.

Reclamation: The process of restoring mined land to a condition established by applicable law. Reclamation
standards vary widely, but usually address issues of ground and surface water, topsoil, final slope gradients,
overburden and revegetation.

Refining: The purification of crude metallic substances.

Reserves: Ore deposits for which we have established a business development plan.

Resources: Ore deposits for which we have not yet established a business development plan.

Sett: Settlement price.

SHG: Special High Grade.

Skarn: Metamorphic zone developed in the contact area around igneous rock intrusions when carbonate
sedimentary rocks are invaded by large amounts of silicon, aluminum, iron and magnesium. The minerals
commonly present in a skarn include iron oxides, calc-silicates, andradite and grossularite garnet, epidote and
calcite. Many skarns also include ore minerals, several productive deposits of copper or other base metals have been
found in and adjacent to skarns.

Tailings: Finely ground rock from which valuable minerals have been extracted by concentration.

Tonne: A unit of weight. One metric tonne equals 2,204.6 pounds. One short tonne equals 2,000 pounds. Unless
otherwise specified in this document, “tonnes” refers to metric tonnes.

Overview

          We are a diversified Peruvian mining company and a major global producer of zinc, silver and lead. We
began operations in the early 1940s and have consistently ranked among the largest producers of these metals globally
every year from 2006 to 2025, according to Wood Mackenzie and GFMS. We were the second-leading producer of
zinc, first in lead and among the top three producers of silver in Peru as of December 2025, according to MINEM. We
believe that the quality of our ore deposits, the efficiency of our operations and our economies of scale make us
competitive among metal producers worldwide.

         Our operations are divided into five main units that currently consist of five underground mines and two open
pit mines in operation, five operating concentrator plants and one leaching plant extending across the Junín and Pasco
departments in Peru, with San Cristobal - Carahuacra the largest mine accounting for approximately 31.7% of our
2025 tonnage production of zinc. Our mining units are all located between 170 and 295 kilometers from Lima, in the
Central Andean region, a center of mining activity in Peru for centuries. As of December 31, 2025, our proven and
probable reserves were 47.2 million tonnes and our measured, indicated and inferred resources were 450.2 million
tonnes, which represented an average mine life of approximately 17 years at 2025 production levels. We have been
granted mining concessions totaling approximately 268,000 hectares, of which: (i) 39.3% are currently being
exploited, (ii) 4.2% are being explored, and (iii) approximately 56.5% remain unexploited and unexplored. In addition
to our mining operations, we also own 864 hectares of land near the Chancay port that we expect to develop directly
or through potential partnerships.

RISK FACTORS

          You should carefully consider the following risk factors, as well as the other information presented in this
offering memorandum, before buying our Notes. The risks and uncertainties described below are not the only ones
that we face. Additional risks and uncertainties that we do not know about or that we currently think are immaterial
may also impair our business operations. Any of the following risks, if they actually occur, could materially and
adversely affect our business, results of operations, prospects and financial condition. In that event, the market
price of the Notes could decline, and you could lose all or part of your investment.

Risks Relating to Our Business

Our business is highly dependent on the price of the metals we produce.

          Our financial performance is significantly affected by the commodity prices of the minerals we produce,
particularly the market prices of zinc, silver, lead and, to a lesser extent, copper and gold. Historically, prices of such
metals have been subject to substantial fluctuations and are affected by numerous factors beyond our control, including
international economic and political conditions, levels of supply and demand, the availability and costs of substitutes,
inventory levels maintained by users, actions of participants in the commodities markets and currency exchange rates.
These factors make future price movements difficult to predict. In addition, the market prices of zinc, silver, lead,
copper, gold and certain other metals have on occasion been subject to rapid short-term changes.

         During the last 3-year period ended March 31, 2026, zinc, silver, lead, copper and gold showed average lows
and highs as follows: zinc US$2,364 per tonne, low in 2024 and US$3,320 per tonne, high in 2026; silver US$21.91
per ounce, low in 2023 and US$92.12 per ounce, high in 2026; lead US$1,879 per tonne, low in 2026 and US$2,252
per tonne, high in 2023; copper US$7,939 per tonne, low in 2023 and US$13,088 per tonne, high in 2026; and gold
US$1,910 per ounce, low in 2023 and US$5,015 per ounce, high in 2026. Future declines in metal prices, and
especially silver, zinc, lead, copper and gold prices, could have an adverse impact on our results of operations and
financial condition, and we might consider curtailing or modifying certain of our operations.

Changes in the demand for the metals we produce could adversely affect our sales volume and revenues.

          Our revenues depend on the volume of metals we sell, which in turn depends on the level of industrial and
consumer demand for these metals. Demand for these metals is mostly driven by: in the case of zinc, consumption of
galvanized steel for construction and infrastructure, the production of brass and die-casting; in the case of silver, its
general perception as a store of value as well as its uses in industrial processes and products, such as batteries, bearings,
brazing and soldering, catalysts, electronics and photographic material, and its use by direct consumers, such as for
jewelry, silverware and coins; in the case of lead, its uses as energy storage and in certain other products such as
chemicals, ammunition, oxides in glass and ceramics, casting metals and sheet lead; in the case of copper, its uses in
the construction industry, electronic product manufacturing, power generation, transmission and distribution, and the
production of industrial machinery; and in the case of gold, its general perception as a store of value as well as global
economic activity outlook. See “Industry Overview.” An increase in the production of these metals world-wide or
changes in technology, industrial processes or consumer habits, including increased demand for substitute materials,
may decrease the demand for these metals. A fall in demand, resulting from economic slow-downs or recessions or
other factors, could also decrease the volume of metals we sell and therefore materially and adversely impact our
results of operations and financial condition.

Our results and financial condition are affected by global and local market conditions which we do not control and
cannot predict.

          We are subject to the risks arising from adverse changes in domestic and global economic and political
conditions. Our industry is cyclical by nature, fluctuates with economic cycles and is impacted by economic
instability.

          If the global economic condition deteriorates it could have an impact on our business and our financial
condition. Continued global economic weakness may prompt banks to limit or deny lending to us or to our customers,
which could have a material adverse effect on our liquidity, on our operations, on our ability to carry out our announced
capital investment programs and may prompt our customers to slow down or reduce the purchase of our products. We
may experience longer sales cycles, difficulty in collecting sales proceeds, and lower prices for our products. We

cannot provide any assurance that any of these events will not have a material adverse effect on market conditions,
the prices of our securities, our ability to obtain financing, and our results of operations and financial condition.

We have incurred losses in the past and may incur losses in the future.

         For the year ended December 31, 2023, our net loss was US$10.0 million. Although we had a net profit of
US$137.1 million in 2024 and a net profit of US$205.4 million in 2025, we may incur losses in the future and there
can be no assurance that we will be able to operate profitably during future periods. If we are unable to operate
profitably during future periods, and are not successful in obtaining additional financing, we could be forced to cease
certain exploration and evaluation programs and mine development activities as a result of insufficient cash resources,
which could adversely affect our business, financial condition and results of operations.

Our operations and results of operations may be affected by international conflicts and terrorist activities.

         Our business and operations may be adversely affected by political tension, hostility and instability caused
by conflicts around the world. It is not possible to predict the broader or longer-term consequences of this risk as it
could end in the expansion of conflicts into adjacent countries, further sanctions, embargoes, regional instability,
geopolitical shifts and adverse effects on macroeconomic conditions, security conditions, fuel prices, critical mining
commodities, transport issues, currency exchange rates and financial, credit and insurance markets, and others.

         For example, sanctions introduced on Russia and Belarus by the EU, UK and U.S. in response to Russia’s
invasion of Ukraine have had, and may continue to have, a disruptive effect on global markets, particularly energy
markets, contributing to volatility in fuel prices and increasing costs for airlines and airport operators.

         Additionally, global markets and supply chains have been, and may continue to be, adversely affected by
the ongoing conflict between Israel and Hamas. While ceasefire agreements have been reached in the past, there are
no assurances that any current or future agreements will hold. The security situation remains fluid, and any renewed
military actions, restrictions, or government-imposed measures could adversely affect our supply chains and
financial condition.

          The Middle East has been further destabilized due to military operations by the United States and Israel
against Iran, including the killing of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and other senior Iranian officials, as
well as retaliatory actions by Iran. Ongoing geopolitical tensions, including the potential for military escalation and
broader regional conflict, may adversely affect economic conditions and create uncertainty that could negatively
impact our business, financial condition and results of operations. In addition, the related virtual closure of shipping
through the Strait of Hormuz has raised concerns about broader disruptions to global energy supply, which could in
turn contribute to elevated inflation and slower economic growth in major economies. As an example, on March 8,
2026, oil prices surged due to the war, reaching US$119.50 a barrel, being that the first time in four years in which

         Since 1991, the Peruvian economy has undergone a major transformation from a highly protected and
regulated system to a free-market economy. During this period, protectionist and interventionist laws and policies
have been gradually dismantled to create a liberal economy led by the private sector and market conditions. The
Peruvian economy has generally performed well under these policies. GDP has grown at an average annual rate of
over 4.26% during the period from 2000 to June 2025, though only grew at an average annual rate of 1.3% from 2020
to 2024, according to the Peruvian Central Bank. Currency exchange controls and restrictions on remittances of profits,
dividends and royalties have ceased. Prior to 1991, Peru exercised control over the foreign currency exchange markets
by imposing multiple exchange rates and placing restrictions on the possession and use of foreign currencies. In 1991,
the Peruvian government eliminated all foreign currency exchange controls and unified exchange rates. Currently,
foreign currency exchange rates are determined by market conditions, with regular purchases of U.S. dollars in the
local market by the Peruvian Central Bank in order to reduce volatility in the value of the sol.

Overview

          We are a diversified Peruvian mining company and a major global producer of zinc, silver and lead. We
began operations in the early 1940s and have consistently ranked among the largest producers of these metals globally
every year from 2006 to 2025, according to Wood Mackenzie and GFMS. We were the second-leading producer of
zinc, first in lead and among the top three producers of silver in Peru as of December 2025, according to MINEM. We
believe that the quality of our ore deposits, the efficiency of our operations and our economies of scale make us
competitive among metal producers worldwide.

         Our operations are divided into five main units that currently consist of five underground mines and two open
pit mines in operation, five operating concentrator plants and one leaching plant extending across the Junín and Pasco
departments in Peru, with San Cristobal - Carahuacra the largest mine accounting for approximately 31.7% of our
2025 tonnage production of zinc. Our mining units are all located between 170 and 295 kilometers from Lima, in the
Central Andean region, a center of mining activity in Peru for centuries. As of December 31, 2025, our proven and
probable reserves were 47.2 million tonnes and our measured, indicated and inferred resources were 450.2 million
tonnes, which represented an average mine life of approximately 17 years at 2025 production levels. We have been
granted mining concessions totaling approximately 268,000 hectares, of which: (i) 39.3% are currently being
exploited, (ii) 4.2% are being explored, and (iii) approximately 56.5% remain unexploited and unexplored. In addition
to our mining operations, we also own 864 hectares of land near the Chancay port that we expect to develop directly
or through potential partnerships.

         In the three months ended March 31, 2026, we had sales of US$361.3 million, net profit of US$71.8 million
and Adjusted EBITDA of US$178.1 million. In the first three months of 2026, zinc represented 37.5%, silver
represented 49.7%, lead represented 7.4%, gold represented 2.7% and copper represented 2.7% of our sales by value.
For the year ended December 31, 2025, we had sales of US$1,180.7 million, net profit of US$205.4 million and
Adjusted EBITDA of US$446.5 million. We had Adjusted EBITDA of US$277.2 million for the year ended December
31, 2023, US$297.5 million for the year ended December 31, 2022, and US$380.6 million for the year ended
December 31, 2021. In 2025, zinc represented 48.6%, silver represented 35.3%, lead represented 10.2%, gold
represented 3.1% and copper represented 2.8% of our sales by value. In 2025, concentrator plants treated 8.6 million
dry tonnes of ore grading on average, 3.5% zinc, 2.2 silver ounces per tonne, 1.0% lead and 0.1% copper, and the
oxides leaching plant treated 1,001 thousand dry tonnes of ore grading 5.9 silver ounces per tonne and 0.5 gold grams
per tonne. We are currently developing projects to expand our production such as Romina, Esperanza, Zoraida,
Carhuacayan, Palma, Santa Barbara and Colquihuarmi. See “Business—Growth Projects.” For a reconciliation of
Adjusted EBITDA to profit for the period/year, see “Selected Consolidated Financial Data.”

Key Factors Affecting Our Business and Results of Operations

          Metal Prices. Our financial performance is significantly affected by the market prices of silver, zinc, lead,
and, to a lesser extent, copper. Metal prices have historically been subject to wide fluctuations and are affected by
numerous factors beyond our control. These factors, which affect each metal to varying degrees, include international
economic and political conditions, levels of supply and demand, the availability and cost of substitutes, inventory
levels maintained by producers and others, and, to a lesser degree, inventory carrying costs and currency exchange
rates. In addition, the market prices of certain metals have on occasion been subject to rapid short-term changes due
to speculative activities. For example, in the first quarter of 2026, metal prices, except for lead, increased compared
to 2025 prices, mainly driven by uncertainty and rising worldwide geopolitical tensions, which supported a broad-

expectations of potential interest rate cuts by the U.S. Federal Reserve. In parallel, the prices for industrial metals also
increased, supported by expectations of tighter demand and the broader macroeconomic environment, where supply
concerns and risk aversion reinforced upward price pressures. The following table sets forth the average published

            The key drivers and recent trends of each of the metals that we produce are:

•           Zinc is a major component of the construction and automotive industries, mainly due to its galvanizing
            applications. Metal prices have exhibited an upward trend since late 2025. This increase has been driven
            primarily by increasingly constrained global supply, smelter production constraints in key markets, persistent
            weakness in the U.S. dollar, and ongoing geopolitical tensions between the United States and Iran.
            Collectively, these factors have contributed to a more supportive and structurally favorable pricing context
            for metals. As of March 31, 2026, the price of zinc was US$3,184 per tonne.

•           Silver is generally seen as store of value and therefore its price tends to be resilient in times of economic
            uncertainty. In addition, applications in electronics and solar cells have added to the already wide spread uses
            of silver in photography, currency, jewelry and silverware. Due to the weakness of the US dollar and rising
            geopolitical uncertainty, silver prices followed the same trend as gold, acting as a safe haven and drawing
            strong investment demand amid market uncertainty to reach all-time highs in the first quarter of 2026. In the
            first three months of 2026, silver prices increased compared to the average price in the first three months of
            2025 from US$31.9 per ounce to an average of US$94.4 per ounce in the first three months of 2026. As of
            March 31, 2026, the price of silver was US$72.7 per ounce.

•           Lead is used as energy storage and in certain other products such as ammunition, oxides in glass and ceramics,
            casting metals and sheet lead. As in the case of zinc, lead prices have also been guided by the growing
            concerns over geopolitical tensions between the United States and Iran. Nonetheless, lead’s demand structure
            differs from that of zinc, resulting in distinct pricing dynamics. From the end of 2021 to the end of 2024, lead
            prices fluctuated in response to evolving market conditions, including developments in automobile demand
            and lead-acid battery consumption across various markets. Demand for lead continues to be supported by its
            use in batteries and energy storage applications. In late 2025 and early 2026, the weakness of the U.S. dollar
            also contributed to a recovery in lead prices. As of March 31, 2026, the price of lead stood at US$1,881 per
            tonne.

•           Copper is used for construction, power generation and transmission, electronic product manufacturing, and
            the production of industrial machinery and transportation vehicles. Similar to the other metals described
            above, the price of copper was also initially negatively impacted at the beginning of 2025 as a result of the
            trade disputes between the United States and China. However, in the final months of 2025 and the beginning
            of 2026, copper prices increased, reaching new highs. This upward movement was supported by strong
            structural demand and tight supply, with a weaker U.S. dollar and Middle East-related supply risks providing
            additional support, though geopolitical tensions also added volatility to the metal’s price performance. As of
            March 31, 2026, the price of copper was US$12,160 per tonne.

          Commercial Terms. The commercial terms that we negotiate for our sales affect our business performance.
We sell our products through long-term contracts and tenders. In 2025, approximately 12.6% of our sales were under
long-term contracts and 87.4% under tenders. Our client base is composed of major global commodity traders and
refineries. We have significant negotiating leverage and typically obtain very competitive commercial terms for our
products. Sales prices for our products are established principally by reference to prices quoted on the London Metal
Exchange and London Bullion Market. Pricing is based on prevailing average prices for the relevant metal for a given
period, generally for the month of shipment, the month following the month of shipment or the second month
following the month of shipment. Revenues are recorded at provisional prices determined at the time of shipment.
Usually, an adjustment is then made after delivery of the products, based on the final pricing terms, the final tonnage
delivered (FOB and CIF tonnages are determined at destination) and the final metal contents delivered. Sales to trading
companies accounted for approximately 76% of our sales by value in 2025 and 71% in the first three months of 2026.

          We take advantage of our leading position in the Central Andes in terms of tonnage and a diversified high
quality product basket. The Central Andes is home to several other major mining operations. As a result, this area is
one of the most important concentrate hubs of the world. In addition, trading companies have a long history in the
region and are generally willing to offer premium terms for our concentrates, as our volume and quality is needed to
offset other producers’ low volumes and especially lower quality concentrates. In general, because of the quality and
volume of our production, we have several alternatives to choose from when placing our sales.

Dividend Policy

         Our dividend policy based on past years’ practice has been to pay approximately 20% of our net profits in
the form of either cash or stock. There are two kinds of dividend payments: (i) provisional dividends, which are
approved by the board of directors and are generally paid during the fourth quarter of each year, and (ii) final
dividends, which are paid in accordance with the annual shareholders’ meeting. However, the amount and timing of
such payments are subject to the final approval at such annual shareholders’ meeting and board of directors’ meeting,
as well as to the availability of earnings to distribute. Peruvian corporations law (Law No. 26887, as amended, Ley
General de Sociedades) establishes a mandatory dividend of 50% or less of the previous year’s after-tax profits, net
of the amount allocated to the legal reserve, if requested by shareholders representing at least 20% of the total common
stock outstanding.

BUSINESS

General

         We are a diversified Peruvian mining company and a major global producer of zinc, silver and lead. We
began operations in the early 1940s, and Wood Mackenzie and GFMS have consistently ranked us among the largest
producers of these metals globally every year since 2006. We were the second-leading producer of zinc, first in lead
and among the top three producers of silver in Peru up to December 2025, according to MINEM. We believe that the
quality of our ore deposits, the efficiency of our operations and our economies of scale make us competitive among
metal producers worldwide.

         Our operations are divided into five main units that currently consist of five underground mines and two open
pit mines in operation, five operating concentrator plants and one leaching plant extending across the Junín and Pasco
departments in Peru, with our largest mine, San Cristobal – Carahuacra, accounting for approximately 31.7% of our
2025 tonnage production of zinc. Our mining units are all located between 170 and 295 kilometers from Lima, in the
Central Andean region, a center of mining activity in Peru for centuries. As of December 31, 2025, our proven and
probable reserves were 47.2 million tonnes and our measured, indicated and inferred resources were 450.2 million

History

         We began operations in 1943 as Volcan Mines Limited, with the Ticlio and Carahuacra mines. In the 1990s,
as part of several privatizations in Peru, the Peruvian government auctioned certain mining areas and related assets.
We acquired several of them and grew at a rapid pace. Over the past 30 years, our most significant asset acquisitions
have included the following:

•                  In 1997, Volcan Mines Limited acquired, via an international public auction, Empresa Minera Mahr Tunel
                   S.A., owner of the Mahr Tunel, San Cristobal and Andaychagua mining operations, from Centromin, which
                   had been Peru’s state mining company since 1974. This acquisition started our expansion process, which
                   resulted in a 400% increase in production. In 1998, Volcan Mines Limited and Empresa Minera Mahr Tunel
                   S.A. merged to create Volcan Compañía Minera S.A.A., our current legal name.

•                  In 1999, we acquired, via an international public auction, Empresa Minera Paragsha from Centromin. This
                   acquisition included the Cerro de Pasco mining operation, which made us the largest zinc mining company
                   in Peru.

•                  In 2000, we acquired Empresa Administradora Chungar S.A.C. and Vinchos, owners of the Animón and
                   Vinchos mines, respectively.

•                  Since 2000, in addition to selectively acquiring other smaller mining operations, we have focused on
                   integrating the companies we acquired, placing emphasis on reducing costs and increasing our reserves and
                   resources. Under the leadership of Dr. Roberto Letts Colmenares, majority shareholder and Chairman of the
                   board until his passing in 2010, we expanded our operations and became the largest silver and lead producer
                   in Peru and the second largest in zinc. At the same time, we became one of the top ten producers in silver,
                   lead and zinc worldwide.

•                  On February 1, 2011, we spun off the assets that comprise our Cerro de Pasco Unit to Empresa
                   Administradora Cerro S.A.C. (“Empresa Administradora Cerro”). In consideration, we received shares

Reserves and Resources

Methodology

          Our mineral resources and mineral reserves follow the guidelines of leading international standards in the
industry such as Australia’s JORC and Canada’s NI 43-101 standard, and are reported under the U.S. Securities and
Exchange Commission’s SK 1300 regulation. This regulatory alignment ensures methodological consistency,
international comparability, and full compliance with best practices for transparency, integrity, and traceability
required by global capital markets.

         The information on reserves and resources as of December 31, 2025 included in this offering memorandum
has been prepared under the general supervision of our chief geological engineer, and our geology and planning
managers, and was found to be in compliance with those international frameworks by SLR Consulting, a widely
recognized international consulting firm in the mining sector. The report produced by SLR Consulting is not,
however, included in this offering memorandum and is not incorporated by reference into this offering
memorandum, and all information on reverses and resources included herein are prepared by our chief geological
engineer and our geology and planning managers, acting as competent persons.

         Mineral resources are veins and ore bodies of economic value that have been identified and evaluated through
exploration, reconnaissance and sampling. Resources are estimated based on geological knowledge about the deposit,
which is based on scientific concepts concerning the formation of minerals such as oxides, sulfides and mixed ores,
as well as available knowledge concerning the geological continuity of the mineralized sectors. This is based on
technical parameters, such as robustness of the genetic-geological model and its validation through drillings.

         Resources may be subdivided further, based on the degree of knowledge that we have of their extent and
composition. If our knowledge of the resources is extensive and direct, they are measured resources; if our knowledge
of them is substantial but less extensive, they are indicated resources; and if our knowledge of them is only indirect,
they are inferred resources. Measured resources are based on a dense grid of regularly distributed drillings, indicated
resources are based on an intermediate grid of regularly distributed drillings, and inferred resources are based on

                                                           69

irregularly, sometimes sporadically distributed drillings, where the continuity of ore grades is mostly supported by
concepts on the theoretical continuity of geological events, such as lithology, alteration and mineralization. Resources
that are either measured or indicated, as opposed to inferred, are sometimes together referred to as demonstrated
resources. Resources of all three categories are sometimes referred to together as identified resources.

          A “reserve” is that part of a mineral resource, which, at the time of determination, may be economically and
legally extracted. Reserve estimates are the result of studies that take into account certain technical, economic and
legal factors, which are not considered when estimating mineral resources. Reserve estimates are based on mineral
resource estimates but also reflect knowledge, at the time of determination, regarding the amount of such resources
that can be recovered and sold at prices in excess of the total costs associated with extraction and processing. Reserve
estimates are adjusted as technical, economic and legal circumstances change. Reserves are typically first determined
at the time of planning a full-scale mining project. As a result, reserves are not reported for certain of our mineral
deposits. Reserves may be “proven” or “probable.” Our proven reserves are based on our measured mineral resources,
while our probable reserves are based on our indicated mineral resources, in each case after undertaking studies
regarding certain technical, economic and legal factors.

          The drilling programs during 2025 were strategically subdivided into (i) exploration drilling, to incorporate
new economically inferred resources and evaluate areas with high geological-economic potential and (ii) infill drilling,
aimed at reclassifying inferred resources to indicated and indicated to measured, with the objective of increasing
geological certainty of the mining plan blocks and replenishing and increasing reserves; that is, dynamically relocating
drilling programs in strategic areas in order to obtain the highest volume of resources that can be converted into
reserves. The development of exploration drilling and infill drilling programs allowed for proper production planning
and ensured long-term sustainability.

         Mineral reserves are the economically mineable portion of a measured and indicated mineral resource whose
mining is viable based on the evaluation of various modifying factors. Reserves include estimates of material dilution,
contingencies for losses that may occur during mining, and associated costs for mining. Reserves are categorized as
either proven or probable based on their degree of certainty.
