Yauli Unit

             General

          The Yauli Unit is located 40 kilometers from the city of La Oroya and 170 kilometers from Lima and is
accessible by road and railway. It is comprised mainly of three underground mines (San Cristobal - Carahuacra,
Andaychagua and Ticlio) producing an aggregate of approximately 3.1 million tonnes per year of ore bearing zinc,
silver, lead and copper. The San Cristobal mine has been recently merged with Carahuacra mine and the previous 154
separate mining concessions are now registered in our name before the Public Registries as a single “San Cristobal –
Carahuacra” concession. The ore is treated at two concentrator plants, Victoria and Andaychagua, with an aggregate
processing capacity of 8,650 tonnes of ore per day. In 2025, this unit produced approximately 162.3 thousand tonnes
of zinc, 6.6 million ounces of silver, 25.3 thousand tonnes of lead, 2.1 thousand tonnes of copper and 4.0 thousand
ounces of gold, representing approximately 63.8% of our sales by value. In the twelve months ended March 31, 2026,
this unit represented approximately 63.7% of our sales by value. In the first three months of 2026, this unit produced
approximately 34.3 thousand tonnes of zinc, 1.3 million ounces of silver, 5.8 thousand tonnes of lead, 0.4 thousand
tonnes of copper and 0.9 thousand ounces of gold, representing approximately 63.1% of our sales by value in the
period, as compared to the approximate production of 39.5 thousand tonnes of zinc, 1.7 million ounces of silver, 6.5
thousand tonnes of lead, 0.7 thousand tonnes of copper and 1.2 thousand ounces of gold in the first three months of
2025. As of December 31, 2025, our proven and probable reserves were 18.9 million tonnes and our measured,
indicated and inferred resources were 53.2 million tonnes. The estimated mine life of the Yauli Unit is approximately
12 years at 2025 production levels, taking into account resources from advanced exploration targets.

Cerro de Pasco Unit

             General

          The Cerro de Pasco Unit is located in the Pasco district, Pasco department, and is accessible from the Central
Highway of Peru, approximately 295 kilometers from Lima. It consists of an open pit mine and mineral stockpiles
producing an aggregate of approximately 3.4 million tonnes per year of ore bearing zinc, silver and lead. The ore is
treated at one concentrator plant, which has an aggregate processing capacity of approximately 12,500 tonnes of ore

Transportation and Shipping

         Once extracted from our mines, ore is transported either by truck or, in the case of our Cerro de Pasco Mining
Unit, by belt to the plants where it will be treated to produce our final product concentrates of zinc, lead and copper.
These concentrates are then further transported, either by truck or railroad depending on the availability thereof as


                                                                       82

well as the plant of origination, to warehouses in the Callao port area, except for a portion of the zinc concentrates that
we allocate to the Cajamarquilla zinc refinery in Huachipa. The Yauli Unit and Cerro de Pasco Unit can easily share
trucks or railcars for such purposes, while the Chungar Unit and Alpamarca Unit currently use trucks. The final
destinations for these concentrates vary and their distribution is managed by our commercial department through a
monthly shipping and delivery program.

         Our doré bars are transported by armored truck from the Cerro de Pasco Mining Unit to the Jorge Chavez
Airport in Lima, where they are subsequently shipped by plane to the country of destination (in most cases,
Switzerland).

        We manage shipping and delivery risk related to the sale of our products according to the following
arrangements:

•        CIP (Carriage and Insurance Paid to) Warehouse.

         We bear the costs and risk associated with delivering concentrates locally to a warehouse. Once the
         delivery trucks have entered that warehouse, the buyer bears further risk and any costs. While these
         concentrates are usually exported afterwards, we do not arrange that process.

•        DAP (Delivered at Place) Warehouse.

         We bear the costs and risk associated with delivering concentrates to a designated place. Upon arrival at
         that destination, the buyer bears further risk and any costs. While these concentrates are usually exported
         afterwards, we typically do not arrange that process. As applicable, the buyer manages custom clearance
         and pays any applicable tariffs.

•        FOB (Free on Board) Callao port.

         We bear the costs and risk associated with delivering concentrates to and storing them at our Callao port
         warehouse. The buyer is responsible for providing a vessel for loading and shipping. Once the concentrates
         have crossed that ship’s rail during loading, the buyer bears further risk and any costs. We arrange the
         relevant export paperwork.

•        CIF (Cost, Insurance and Freight) “Discharge Port.”

         We bear the costs and risk associated with delivering concentrates to and storing them at our Callao port
         warehouse. We are responsible for arranging a vessel for loading and shipping. Once the concentrates have
         crossed that ship’s rail during loading, the buyer bears further risk and any costs. We arrange the relevant
         export paperwork.

Sales & Marketing

          We sell our products through long-term contracts and tenders. In 2025, approximately 12.6% of our sales
were under long-term contracts and 87.4% under tenders. Our ability to produce and deliver significant volumes makes
us a significant supplier to a broad client base composed of major global commodity traders and refineries. As a result,
we have significant negotiating leverage, and we typically obtain very competitive sales conditions, including
commercial terms, for our products.

         Sales prices for our products are established principally by reference to prices quoted on the London Metal
Exchange and London Bullion Market. Pricing is based on prevailing average prices for the relevant metal for a given
period, which generally constitutes the month of shipment or the first or second month following. Revenues are
recorded at provisional prices determined at the time of shipment. Usually, an adjustment is then made after delivery
of the products, based on the final pricing terms, the final tonnage delivered (in FOB and CIF arrangements, tonnages
are commonly determined at the destination) and the final metal contents delivered.

          Sales to trading companies accounted for approximately 75.97% of our sales by value in 2025 and 71.35%
in the first three months of 2026. Sales to smelters accounted for approximately 24.03% of our sales by value in 2025
and 28.65% in the first three months of 2026.

is open to the northwest and southwest, and geophysical studies confirm the continuity of the mineralized zones in

Northern Cluster

          The Northern Cluster is anchored by the Animón mine of the Chungar Unit, where brownfield and step-out

zone of the Animón mine. Initial discovery occurred in 2019, when a 125-meter economic intercept with zinc and
copper mineralization was identified in proximity to the Animón mine. Exploration was restarted in 2020 with 959
meters of diamond drilling, confirming the continuity of the orebody toward the southeast.

         Between late 2020 and 2021, an additional 5,684 meters of diamond drilling were completed, establishing
the geometry of the mineralized body and confirming economic metal content. Mineralization remained open in all
directions upon completion of this phase.

        In 2022, the most intensive drilling campaign to that point was executed, totaling 26,091 meters dedicated to
Esperanza. In 2023, an 18,874-meter campaign was executed from both surface and underground platforms,

        In 2025, the Esperanza geological model was reinterpreted as a polymetallic massive replacement deposit.
According to the new model, the potential mineral inventory is estimated at 53 million tonnes, with average grades of
5.2% zinc, 0.63% copper, and 0.50 silver ounces per tonne.

Resurgidora

         Resurgidora is a skarn hosted massive replacement body located immediately beneath Esperanza, at a depth
of approximately 900 meters below current Animón operations. Discovered through deeper drilling executed during
the 2022 and 2023 campaigns, the deposit intersects copper, zinc, and silver mineralization within a widely developed
skarn zone that is open in all directions and at depth. The geological characteristics are comparable to those at
Antamina, indicating significant potential for resource expansion. Certain sectors also display anomalous values of
molybdenum, tin, and tungsten, suggesting an associated porphyry-type mineralization environment. Between 2019
and 2020, an initial program, comprising 10 diamond drill holes, was completed.

         In 2025, a comprehensive reinterpretation of the Resurgidora geological model was completed, enabling
more reliable delineation of massive replacement zones within carbonate units proximal to the intrusive body. This
work produced a geological envelope fully consistent with a skarn-type deposit model. According to the new model,
the potential mineral inventory is estimated at 80 million tonnes at grades of 1.5% zinc, 0.8% copper, and 0.8 silver
ounces per tonne, with the mineralized system remaining open in all directions and at depth.

         Techo Esperanza

         Techo Esperanza is a polymetallic massive replacement body situated 300 meters below the current Animón
operation, hosted in skarn zones and located in close proximity to active mining infrastructure. Between 2019 and
2022, six diamond drill holes were completed which confirmed replacement bodies with significant zinc and silver
grades. A deep drill hole in this sector also intersected copper, zinc, and silver replacement bodies in skarn zones
analogous to Resurgidora, as well as vein-type structures consistent with the veins currently in operation, indicating
their continuity up to 400 meters below current operations.

         In 2025, the exploration campaign was reactivated with an updated geological model and revised resource
estimation. Techo Esperanza is estimated to contain potential resources of 7.8 million tonnes at 4.9% zinc, 0.14%
copper, and 2.0 silver ounces per tonne. An additional exploration potential has been identified toward the northern
extension of the mineralized body.

         The Romina Mining District, located in central Peru, hosts the Puagjanca, Andrea, Adriana, Santa, and

the surrounding targets also offer significant medium-term growth potential.

         Andrea, Adriana, and Esperanza Sur are polymetallic exploration targets located along a North-Northwest-
trending structural alignment associated with the axis of a regional anticline, reinforcing the structural control and
continuity of the mineralized system.

         In 2025, exploration was reinitiated across all three targets through diamond drilling, accompanied by a
comprehensive geological reinterpretation and updated resource estimation. As a result, inferred resources of 6.3
million tonnes were established at grades of 3.56% zinc and 0.17 silver ounce per tonne, with an exploration potential
exceeding 8.4 million tonnes at grades of 3.20% zinc and 0.20 silver ounce per tonne. Mineralization remains open

Amortization of development expenses

          Development expenses consist of investments of sums of money incurred by mining companies before
starting the production stage and the legislator has given special treatment to such investments. Article 75 of the
Supreme Decree No. 014-92-EM (“General Mining Law”) allows companies to deduct development expenses in the
year in which they are produced or amortized within a maximum period of three years; however, it does not indicate
that they must be amortized proportionally or linearly. For as long as we have operated in Peru, we have amortized
these expenses in accordance with the indicated law; that is, for the maximum period of three years, without any other
restriction.

         According to the Peruvian national tax authority (Superintendencia Nacional de Aduanas y de
Administración Tributaria, or “SUNAT”), development expenses must be amortized linearly, despite the lack of
specific regulation governing this specific point. The Company and certain of its subsidiaries have had their
amortization schedules challenged by SUNAT.

         Compañía Minera Chungar has obtained a favorable ruling of the Supreme Court in this matter, in which the
Court recognized that its development expenses could be amortized without any restriction other that the maximum
term of three years. However, other companies in our economic group still face disputes on this issue. Since 2018, the
Company and its subsidiaries have started amortizing development expenses linearly, preventing new challenges from
SUNAT in connection with this matter in the future.

Losses sustained from transactions with derivative financial instruments that have no hedging purpose

          Pursuant to article 5-A of Supreme Decree No. 179-2004 EF (“Income Tax Law”), a loss derived from
derivative financial instruments can only be considered for tax purposes a deductible loss if it has a hedging purpose.
According to the Income Tax Law, a derivative financial instrument has a hedging purpose if, among others, the
following requirements are met: (i) the asset or liability hedged must be identified, (ii) the risk to be hedged must be
specific; and (iii) the derivative financial instruments must be entered into or subscribed in a publicly recognized


                                                           96

market. The Company, Empresa Administradora Cerro and Compañía Minera Chungar have entered into or subscribed
several derivative financial instruments in the form of a swap in order to cover the risk of the downward trend in zinc
and lead prices. At the time of liquidation of such derivative financial instruments, deductible losses were generated
for tax purposes.

          SUNAT concluded that the Company, Empresa Administradora Cerro and Compañía Minera Chungar did
not submit sufficient documentation to prove the identification of the covered sales and the specific risk, as required
by the Income Tax Law. SUNAT also concluded that the Company, Empresa Administradora Cerro and Compañía
Minera Chungar did not comply with requirement (iii) above because the underlying prices agreed to under the swap
agreements were not published in the London Metal Exchange (LME). For those reasons, SUNAT disqualified the
loss that resulted from those derivative financial instruments as deductible for tax purposes.

        The Company, Empresa Administradora Cerro and Compañía Minera Chungar have challenged these
SUNAT objections before the Administrative Tax Court. As of the date of this offering memorandum, the
Administrative Tax Court has not yet rendered a decision on the matter.

INDUSTRY OVERVIEW

Zinc Industry

Overview

         Zinc is an internationally traded commodity. The London Metal Exchange is recognized as its principal
trading market. Prices generally reflect the worldwide zinc supply and demand balance, but can also be influenced by
the activities of speculative market participants such as investment funds and by fluctuations in currency exchange
rates.

         An important characteristic of zinc is its resistance to corrosion, which makes it a versatile metal.
Additionally, its low melting point, fluidity, non-magnetic propensity, strength and alloying properties have increased
its general demand across various applications. Its capacity as a surface treatment has proved crucial in protecting
steel products against corrosion and improving their durability. The primary end-use applications of zinc include:
construction (zinc is a major additive in galvanized steel), transportation and automobiles, white goods, industrials
goods and equipment. Currently, there are limited low-cost substitutes for zinc in several of these applications.

Zinc Demand

          Galvanizing is the predominant first-use for zinc, accounting for approximately 60.0% of global zinc usage
in all forms in 2025. The next largest use of zinc is zinc alloys, accounting for 13.0% of total demand, followed by
usage in brass production at 11.0%. 9.0% of zinc compounds is used in producing oxides and chemicals and a further
5.0% of zinc usage involves its conversion into rolled and extruded semi-manufactured products. In both absolute and
percentage terms, galvanizing is forecast to be the fastest growing end-use, with principal applications in the
construction and automotive industries.

          The largest end-use sector for zinc is construction, which, together with publicly-funded infrastructure
activity, accounted for 50.0% of global end-use zinc consumption in 2025. The second most important end-use sector
is transport, which accounted for 21.0% of zinc consumption. Infrastructure represented 16.0% of consumption and
the remainder was used mostly in household appliances.

Silver Industry

Overview

         Silver is one of the eight precious, or noble, metals; the others are gold and the six platinum-group metals.
Silver occurs naturally in its solid metallic state and is commonly associated with deposits of zinc, copper, lead and
gold.

          Silver is distinct from other precious metals in that it is both an industrial and a monetary asset. Silver’s value
is driven by two main factors: first, silver has a number of distinctive physical and chemical properties that make it an
essential and hard-to-substitute component in several industrial applications, and second, in times of economic
uncertainty, silver is viewed as an attractive hedge against inflation and a decrease in value of, among others, the U.S.
dollar.

Silver Demand

         Silver has solid supply and demand fundamentals, with significant demand coming from diverse sectors.
Industrial applications, consumer use and investment are the three main demand drivers. According to the World
Silver Survey, in 2025, industrial, consumer and investment represented 58.0%, 23.0% and 19.0% of silver industrial
demand, respectively.

          According to the World Silver Survey, total global demand for industrial and consumer end-uses, which is
in the form of manufactured end-products, decreased by 5.2% in 2025, to 913.0 million ounces. Similarly, according
to the World Silver Survey, the consumer category decreased by 10.0% to 256.0 million ounces in 2025.

         China is the largest global silver marketplace, fueling significant industrial and consumer demand. China’s
rapid population and income growth, surging demand for consumer electronics and promising housing market are
driving its silver demand. According to World Silver Survey, industrial demand for silver in China has risen from
150.9 million ounces in 2010 to 282.9 million ounces in 2025, an increase of 87.5%.

Industrial Demand

          Traditional industrial applications of silver include batteries, bearings, brazing and soldering, catalysts and
electronics. Silver’s electrical and thermal conductive properties make it ideal for multiple high-performance
electronics and high voltage circuits, connectors and other electrical components. Silver’s increased use in emerging
applications, as opposed to otherwise traditional industrial uses, is expected to continue to augment industrial demand.
Emerging applications include utilizing silver’s reflectivity as a component in solar cells to produce “green”
electricity, utilizing silver’s antimicrobial properties in medical applications and in the prevention of algae build-up
in water purification systems.

         According to the World Silver Survey, industrial demand for silver rose by 124.5% between 2017 and 2025
to 657.0 million ounces.

Consumer Demand

          Jewelry and silverware are the main consumer uses of silver. The fabrication of these products relies on
silver’s luster, resistance to tarnishing and malleability. According to the World Silver Survey, this sector accounted
for 20.0% of total demand for silver in 2025.

          In 2025, photographic uses accounted for 2.1% of total silver demand, according to the World Silver Survey.
However, photographic off-take has been on a steady decline since 2001, driven by the move from silver halide to
digital technology, especially in the area of consumer film.

         According to the World Silver Survey, between 2024 and 2025, consumer demand for silver decreased by
10.0%, to 256.0 million ounces. A major source of the decrease in consumer demand for silver in 2025 was in jewelry.

Investment Demand

        Investment demand for silver has increased from 2024 to 2025. According to the World Silver Survey, net
investment in silver increased to 218.0 million ounces in 2025, up 12.0% from 2024 levels.

Silver Supply

          Silver supply derives from two principal sources: mine production and scrap supply. According to the World
Silver Survey, mine production in 2025 comprised 78.0% of total silver supply, while scrap silver constituted 18.0%
of total silver supply. According to the World Silver Survey, silver mine production increased by 7.0% in 2025.

Overview

         Lead has an estimated abundance of almost one-sixth that of zinc, with which it is commonly geologically

in 2025. It can be subdivided into two groups, including:

•         SLI (Starting-Lighting-Ignition) batteries currently account for over half of all lead demand. These are mainly

Copper Industry

Overview

          Copper is an internationally traded commodity, and its price is largely determined on the major metals
exchanges. Like zinc prices, copper prices generally reflect the worldwide copper supply and demand balance but can
also be influenced by the activities of speculative market participants and by movements in currency exchange rates.

          Copper is a ductile, corrosion resistant and malleable metal that is an excellent conductor of heat and
electricity and has significant structural capabilities. The primary applications for copper include electronics
applications, electrical conduit, construction and transportation industries, industrial equipment, and consumer
products. While other materials compete with copper for various uses, substitution is modest because of copper’s
unique characteristics.




                                                          103

Copper Demand

         The world’s consumption of copper has increased significantly in the past five years, as large developing
countries enter the global market. Population and industrial growth will continue to be the primary driver of demand
for copper. The rate of industrialization, especially in China and India, has created a high level of copper demand over
the past decade, while metal use in many developing countries remains a fraction of the intensity observed in
developed nations.

       Copper consumption is largely associated with industrial production and tends to follow economic cycles.
Demand for copper products tends to increase during expansion phases, which often leads to price increases.

        Asian refined copper consumption, led by China, has been particularly strong, increasing by a CAGR of
3.7%, compared to a global rate of 2.7% since 2021.

Copper Supply

         While the earth’s crust contains an almost inexhaustible supply of copper, most of it cannot be extracted
economically utilizing existing technologies. Worldwide copper supply is driven by production rates at copper mines
around the globe, as well as a small amount of scrap metal that is available for reuse. According to the USGS Mineral
Commodity Summaries 2026, based upon total copper mined in 2025, the world’s largest producers were Chile
(23.0%), Democratic Republic of the Congo (14.0%), Peru (12.0%), China (8.0%) and Russia (6.0%).

REGULATORY FRAMEWORK

Mining and Processing Concessions

         The General Mining Law (Texto Único Ordenado de la Ley General de Minería) approved by Supreme
Decree No. 014-92-EM, published in the Peruvian Official Gazette, El Peruano, on June 4, 1992, is the primary law
governing both metallic and non-metallic mining activities in Peru and is supplemented by implementing guidelines,
regulations and policies regarding mining and the processing of minerals enacted by MINEM. Under the General
Mining Law, mining activities (except reconnaissance, prospecting, and trade) are carried out exclusively through
various forms of concessions. A concession provides its titleholder with the exclusive right to undertake a specific
mining activity within a determined area.

         There are four types of concessions:

•        Mining concession: grants the right to explore and exploit mineral resources (either metallic or non-metallic).

•        Processing concession: grants the right to extract and concentrate minerals and, to purify, melt and refine
         metals.

•        General works concession or mining labor: grants the right to give auxiliary services to two or more mining
         concessions.

•        Mining transportation concession: grants the right to install and operate a massive transportation system of
         mineral products provided the transportation is not conventional.

         Large and medium scale mining concessions are granted by the INGEMMET, while the other types of
concessions are granted by the DGM. Any act, transfer, termination, or agreement related to these concessions must
be registered with the Mining Rights Book, which is part of the Peruvian Public Registry, to be effective against the
Peruvian government and third parties.

          In Peru, as in many other countries, a mining concession is a special type of real property, different and
separate from the surface land where it is located. Consequently, holding a mining concession does not grant the
titleholder any right to the surface land. To commence mining activities, an authorization from the DGM is required,
which in turn requires having a title over the surface land. (property right, lease, mining easement, authorization to
use or similar valid title to use such land) granted by the owner of the land.

          Holders of concessions or mining claims must comply with several obligations, including the payment of an
annual validity fee (derecho de vigencia) of US$3.00 per applicable hectare in the case of large and medium scale
mining. The annual validity fee is due and payable on or prior to June 30 of each year. Failure to pay the annual
validity fee for two years, consecutive or not, will result in the forfeiture of the mining concession.

         Mining concessions are required to achieve the minimum production level in accordance with the following
rules:

•        The minimum annual production levels for large- and medium-scale mining, equivalent to 1 Peruvian tax
         unit (S/5,500.00 for 2026, approximately US$1,600) per year per hectare, in the case of metallic concessions,
         and 10% of 1 Peruvian tax unit (approximately US$160) per year per hectare, in the case of nonmetallic
         mining concessions.

•        The minimum annual production level is to be achieved no later than the end of the tenth year from the year
         of grant.

•        If the minimum annual production level is not achieved within that period, an annual penalty shall be paid.
         The following rules for calculating the amount of the penalty apply:

             o    If the minimum annual production level is not achieved until the end of the tenth year from the year
                  following the granting of the concession, a mining penalty equivalent to 2% of the corresponding
                  annual production level per year per hectare shall be paid.


                                                         106

o   If the minimum annual production level is not achieved until the end of the fifteenth year from the
                  year following the granting of the concession, a mining penalty equivalent to 5% of the
                  corresponding annual production level per year per hectare shall be paid.

              o   If the minimum annual production level is not achieved until the end of the twentieth year from the
                  year following the granting of the concession, a mining penalty equivalent to 10% of the
                  corresponding annual production level per year per hectare shall be paid.

              o   If the minimum annual production level is not achieved by the end of the thirtieth year from the year
                  following the granting of the concession, the mining concession will be cancelled. In the case of
                  mining concessions granted before 2008, the 30th year term began on January 1, 2009.

        The annual penalty must be paid prior to June 30 of each year. Failure to pay the annual penalty for two years
consecutive, or not, results in the forfeiture of the mining concession.

         The holders of mining concessions are not required to pay the annual penalty fee if they invest at least 10
times the amount of the respective penalty fee per year and per hectare.

        To comply with the minimum production level or minimum investment, the holders of mining concessions
can group concessions into economic management units (Unidades Económicas Administrativas). In order to form an
economic management unit, the mining concessions must be located within a radius ranging from 5, 10 and 20
kilometers depending on the type of mineral exploited. The formation of an economic management unit requires an
approval resolution issued by INGEMMET.

         Finally, titleholders of mining concessions that are in exploration, construction, operation or closure phase,
must file every year a Consolidated Annual Statement (Declaración Anual Consolidada) with the DGM. The
Consolidated Annual Statement that contains information in connection with investments is required on an annual
basis (before April 30 of each year) and the Consolidated Annual Statement that contains information in connection
with production is required on an annual basis (before June 30 of each year). As of the date of this offering
memorandum, we primarily owned metallic mining concessions with respect to zinc, silver, lead, and cooper.
Substantially all of our concessions were granted prior to 2008. Our mining rights and concessions are in full force
and effect under applicable Peruvian laws. We believe that we are in compliance in all material respects with the terms
and requirements applicable to our mining rights and concessions.

Environmental Matters

         In 2005, Peru enacted the General Environmental Law (Law No. 28611), which establishes the main
environmental guidelines and principles applicable in Peru. Pursuant to the General Environmental Law, MINAM
issued national environmental regulations, which have gradually replaced prior guidelines governing governmental
agencies environmental competencies. All environmental studies for exploration activities are evaluated by the
General Directorate of Environmental Mining Affairs of the MINEM (Dirección de Asuntos Ambientales Mineros or
“DGAAM”). The agency in charge of Environmental Certification (Servicio Nacional de Certificación Ambiental
para las Inversiones Sostenibles or “SENACE”) evaluates the exploitation and beneficiation environmental studies
for large- and medium-scale mining. In addition, the OEFA is responsible for supervising the fulfillment of
environmental obligations including commitments approved in environmental assessments studies. If the holder of a
mining concession fails to comply with any obligation related to environmental matters, OEFA can levy a sanction
for such breach with fines of up to 30,000 Peruvian Tax Units (approximately US$47,965,116.30). An entity cannot
be fined more than 10% of the gross annual income it received in the year prior to the date the infraction was
committed.

          According to the Environmental Regulations for Mining Exploration Activities approved by Supreme Decree
042-2017-EM, exploration activities fall into two categories: Category I and Category II. Category I exploration
activities are those involving no more than 40 drilling platforms or affecting an area measuring of up to 10 hectares in
size or the construction of tunnels of up to 100 meters long, while Category II exploration activities are those involving
between 40 and 700 drilling platforms and affecting an area measuring greater than 10 hectares, the construction of
tunnels of up to more than 100 meters long or a pilot plan. For Category I exploration activities, an Environmental
Impact Statement (Declaración de Impacto Ambiental or “DIA”) is required. For Category II exploration activities,
an Environmental Impact Assessment semi-detailed (Estudio de Impacto Ambiental semi-detallado or “EIAsd” is


                                                           107

required and incorporates technical, environmental, and social matters. The approval of DIAs and EIAsd may require
the prior favorable opinion of some competent authorities, such as the National Service of Natural Areas Protected by
the State (Servicio Nacional de Áreas Naturales Protegidas por el Estado, or “SERNANP”) for exploration activities
performed within protected natural areas or their buffer zones.

          In addition, the new regulation requires only an Environmental Technical Report (Ficha Técnica Ambiental
or “FTA”), which is a complementary environmental assessment, for exploration activities involving a maximum of
twenty platforms and which, due to their location and/or characteristics, are expected to generate non-significant
negative environmental impacts. By Resolution No. 237-2024-MINEM/DM, the MINEM approved two types of FTA:
(i) a standard FTA, which allows up to twenty platforms; and (ii) the simplified FTA, which allows up to ten platforms
and to affect an area of up to five hectares.

          Exploration, exploitation and/or processing activities must start within a maximum of five years following
the date that the DIA, EIAsd or EIAd is approved. The DIA, the EIAsd and the FTA, as applicable, must be approved
before exploration activities begin. Any commitments assumed by mining companies in a DIA, EIAsd or FTA are
mandatory and, if they are not fulfilled, OEFA has the authority to fine non-compliant mining companies or suspend
their activities.

          The regulation also provides that the holder of mining activities will perform specified progressive closure,
final closure, and post closure activities during and after exploration programs, exploitation and/or processing
activities. In addition, fines can be imposed if exploration programs begin before the DIA, the EIAsd and the FTA are
approved.

         Holders of mining concessions or mining activities that have completed the exploration stage, or envisage
mining development and exploitation activities (including the processing of minerals), are required to prepare and
obtain the approval of an EIAd from SENACE, which involves, among others, a process of public hearings in the
locations where the project will be developed.

       A modification to the environmental assessment will be required prior to conducting mining activities that
may generate new moderate or negative environmental impacts.

         In addition, according to the Public Participation Regulations in the Mining Subsector approved by Supreme
Decree No. 028-2008-EM, for purpose of preparing the EIA holders of mining concessions must gather and analyze
the social, environmental and economic concerns of the population that lives or works in the areas surrounding the
project prior to the authorization of any activity.

         Holders of mining concessions must undertake steps for public participation prior to and during the
preparation of the DIA, EIAsd and EIAd subject to evaluation as well as during the process of evaluation by DGAAM
(DIA and EIAsd) or SENACE (EIAd). In this process, holders of a mining project are required to submit a public
participation plan, detailing the public participation mechanisms to be executed.

        Supreme Decree 054-2013-PCM was enacted in 2013 to promote investment projects. It allows companies
to only submit a supporting technical report (Informe Técnico Sustentatorio or “ITS”), to modify ancillary
components, capacity expansions, or introduce technological improvements in exploration and exploitation activities.
Although regulation requires that the responsible authority must evaluate the ITS within no more than 15 working
days from the date of submission, this deadline has not been strictly applied in the past.

           According to the Mining Closure Law (Law No. 28090) holders of mining concessions who wish to initiate
mining exploitation activities, as well as those in operation, are required to prepare and submit a mining closure plan
one year after their EIA has been approved. The mining closure plan must contain a description of the steps that will
be taken to restore the areas and facilities of each mining unit they are going to operate. Holders of mining project are
required to secure completion of the final closure and post-closure measures by means of the following guarantees:
(i) letters of credit; (ii) surety bond and similar types of insurance, without the benefit of excussio issued by local or
foreign first category insurance companies; (iii) trust, trust over cash flows, trusts over movable and immovable assets
(other than mining concessions and the facilities covered by the Mine Closure Plan), as well as securities excluding
those issued by the mining activity holder; (iv) joint and several guarantees, based on the previous mentioned
arrangements, without the benefit of excussio; or (v) bank certificates, letters of credit, and stand-by letters of credit
issued by local or foreign first category banking entities.


                                                           108

Supreme Decree No. 042-2017-EM also requires mining companies that perform exploration activities to
conduct closing activities in accordance with the approved environmental assessment, subject to deferral under certain
circumstances. For exploration activities that involve underground works, depending on the volume and features of
the material removed, a closure plan shall be submitted by the mining company following the terms and conditions of
Supreme Decree Nº 033-2005-EM, as amended from time to time.

         Law No. 28271, Law that Regulates the Environmental Liabilities of Mining Activities (Ley que Regula los
Pasivos Ambientales de la Actividad Minera), came into force on July 7, 2004 and serves to regulate the identification
of environmental liabilities and financial responsibility for remediation in mining activities, in each case to mitigate
any negative impact mining may have with respect to the health of the population, environment and property. Pursuant
to Law No. 28271, the DGM will identify environmental liabilities and the entities responsible for their remediation,
which must submit an Environmental Liabilities Closure Plan to the DGAAM. This law also allows voluntary
remediation of environmental liabilities by any person or entity even if these parties are not holders of mining
concessions.

         Finally, we anticipate that additional laws and regulations relating to environmental matters will be enacted
over time. The development of more stringent environmental regulations in Peru could impose additional constraints
and additional costs on our operations that would require us to make significant additional capital expenditures in the
future.

Agriculture Communities and Indigenous People

         Peru has ratified ILO Convention No. 169 concerning Indigenous and Tribal Peoples in Independent
Countries through Legislative Resolution No. 26253. This convention gives indigenous and tribal peoples the right to
previous consultation. As a result, on September 7, 2011, Law No. 29785 on the Right to Prior Consultation of the
Indigenous Population was published. This law, which came into force on 7 December 2011, establishes a prior
consultation procedure for an indigenous population whose collective rights may be directly affected by a legislative
or administrative measure. The Regulations of Law No. 29785 were approved by Supreme Decree No. 001-2012-MC,
which entered into force on April 4, 2012. This regulation specifies the form and circumstances of the required
consultation and the manner in which the agreements will be formalized and provides for a consultation process that
should not last more than 120 calendar days, a term which is not observed in practice.

          In 2019, the Ministerial Resolution No. 403-2019-MINEM/DM was issued, which establishes the
administrative procedures of the Mining Sector that require prior consultation – in the event that such procedures
directly affect indigenous communities – which are: (i) concession of processing; (ii) authorization to commence or
restart exploration, development or exploitation activities; (iii) transport of minerals; and (iv) concessions for general
works and mining labor.

        The consultation procedures are carried out by the General Office of Social Management (“OGGS”) of the
MINEM before the granting of the corresponding authorization or concession by the DGM. Indigenous peoples do
not have the right to veto or stop a mining project. Once this prior consultation procedure has been completed, the
Peruvian Government may approve or reject the applicable legislative or administrative measures at its discretion.

         In addition, the sale, lease, or other disposition of surface lands owned by agriculture or native communities
is subject to the approval of at least two thirds of all community members.

Permits and Licenses

Explosives

        The use of explosives for civil use is regulated by Law No. 30299 and its regulations. Under such law, mining
companies are required to obtain the following permits to operate and store explosives from the National
Superintendence of Security Services, Guns, Munitions and Explosives of Civil Use (Superintendencia Nacional de
Control de Servicios de Seguridad, Armas, Municiones y Explosivos de Uso Civil or “SUCAMEC”):

•        Authorization for the acquisition and use of explosives (Autorización para la adquisición y uso de explosivos
         y materiales relacionados).



                                                           109

•        Authorization for the storage of explosives (Autorización para el almacenamiento de explosivos y materiales
         relacionados).

•        Authorization of the manipulation of explosives for each individual that intends to handle explosives
         (Autorización para la manipulación de explosivos y materiales relacionados).

Water, wastewaters, and emissions

          To use water resources in a mining project, it is necessary to obtain a water right granted by the National
Water Authority (Autoridad Nacional del Agua or “ANA”) prior to the use of underground or fresh water sources. If
the proposed activities will generate domestic or industrial wastewaters discharged into natural water sources or dry
creeks, it is necessary to obtain an authorization granted by the ANA, with the favorable opinion of the General Bureau
of Environmental Health (Dirección General de Salud Ambiental or “DIGESA”).

          In 1996, MINEM issued regulations which established the first maximum permissible levels (“LMPs”) of (i)
liquid effluents emissions and (ii) elements and compounds present in gaseous emissions resulting from mining
activities. Mines and processing plants that were in operation before May 1993 were required to submit Environmental
Adaptation and Management Programs, or PAMAs, that set forth plans to ensure compliance with LMPs. The first
General Water Law was enacted in 1969. In 2008 and 2010, MINAM enacted new water quality standards and new
LMPs for liquid effluents, and, in 2009, all Peruvian mining companies were required to submit updated environmental
management plans that complied with water quality standards and new LMPs for liquid effluents to MINEM. By the
end of 2015, Supreme Decree No. 015-2015 - MINAM was enacted, modifying water quality standards and
establishing supplementary provisions related to compliance. In 2017, Environmental Quality Standards (Estándares
de Calidad Ambiental or “ECAs”) for water were modified by Supreme Decree No. 004-2017-MINAM. Permissible
maximum limits approved in 2010 by Supreme Decree No. 010-2010-MINAM are still valid.

Solid waste and soil contamination

         Within Peru’s mining–environmental regime, environmental certification for large-scale mining projects is
granted by the National Service of Environmental Certification for Sustainable Investments (SENACE) through a
Detailed Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA-d) and its amendments. Environmental oversight and enforcement
rest with the OEFA, which covers assessment, supervision, enforcement, and sanctions. MINEM, through the
DGAAM, issues sector regulations and manages the regime for Mining Environmental Liabilities (PAM). The
Supervisory Agency for Investment in Energy and Mining (OSINERGMIN) oversees safety and technical-operational
aspects of mining infrastructure and components; this role does not replace OEFA’s environmental enforcement.

          Under Peru’s legal framework, waste management obligations cover both non-mining solid waste and mining
waste. For non-mining solid waste and hazardous waste, Legislative Decree 1278 and its Regulations (Supreme Decree
014-2017-MINAM) require application of the 5R hierarchy (Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Recycle and Recover), source
segregation, safe temporary storage, engagement of authorized Solid Waste Operator companies (Empresas
Operadoras de Residuos Sólidos or “EO-RS”), use of Hazardous Solid Waste Manifests (MRSP), annual reporting,
full traceability, and certification of recovery or final disposal. For mining waste, including tailings and waste rock,
Supreme Decree 040-2014-EM and the commitments in the approved Detailed Environmental Impact Assessment
(EIA-d) govern the design, operation, monitoring, and closure of tailings storage facilities (TSFs) and waste-rock
dumps (WRDs) to ensure physical and geochemical stability, with periodic reporting.

        For soil protection in Peru, the Environmental Quality Standards for Soil (EQS), established by Supreme
Decree 011-2017-MINAM and complemented by Supreme Decree 012-2017-MINAM on contaminated-site
management criteria, serve as the binding reference to determine contamination; site management follows a staged
process comprising identification and characterization, risk assessment, selection of remediation technologies,
implementation, verification, and post-closure. A transitional regime under Supreme Decree 002-2013-MINAM, as
complemented by Supreme Decree 002-2014-MINAM, applied to pre-existing Environmental Management
Instruments (Instrumentos de Gestión Ambiental or “IGAs”) until they were updated.

         Regarding PAM in Peru, Law No. 28271 and Supreme Decree 059-2005-EM provides that if a responsible

Cultural heritage protection

         If the design and development of mining projects involve the removal of topsoil, companies need to have a
Surface Archaeological Survey (Diagnóstico Arqueológico de Superficie or “DAS”) conducted and certified by a
licensed archaeologist or obtain from the Ministry of Culture a Certificate of Non-Existence of Archeological Ruins
(Certificado de Inexistencia de Restos Arqueológicos or “CIRA”) and the authorization to perform an Archeological
Monitoring Plan (Plan de Monitoreo Arqueológico or “PMAR”) with respect to the area that is going to be used in
the construction process or in developing the relevant mining project. DAS and CIRA will certify that on the surface
of the evaluated area no archaeological sites or features were discovered. The PMAR involves an archaeological
monitoring by, at least, one archaeological professional, while works are performed seeking to prevent, avoid, control,
reduce and mitigate possible negative impacts on archaeological evidence found in the soil and subsoil. A PMAR is
required prior to initiating works involving soil removal.

          If any archaeological artifacts are accidentally discovered during the construction works or due to any natural
cause, the mining company must stop the construction work immediately and notify the Ministry of Culture. Failure
to stop the construction work will generate applicable civil and criminal liabilities.

Mining Regulatory Contributions

         In Peru, the regulatory contribution (Aporte por Regulación, “APR”) is a mandatory contribution-type tax
that funds sector regulators, capped at 1% of a company’s annual invoicing, net of VAT. It applies to medium and
large mining companies on a monthly self-assessment basis, with enrollment in the relevant APR registries and
exposure to fines for non-compliance and is distinct from royalties that finance regional development.

        For OSINERGMIN, the APR finances safety, technical oversight, and tariff regulation functions in mining,
with the 2026 contribution set at 0.11% of monthly invoicing (excluding VAT). For OEFA, the APR supports
environmental supervision and enforcement in mining, with the 2026 rate at 0.07% of monthly invoicing (excluding
VAT) (still within the 1% legal ceiling), and monthly declarations and payments monitored for compliance.

Safety

         As a mining company, we are subject to both the General Occupational Safety and Health Law (Ley de
Seguridad y Salud en el Trabajo) approved by Law No. 29783, as amended by Law No. 30222, and the relevant
regulations on safety and health applicable to mining activities approved by Supreme Decree No. 055-2010-EM,
subsequently repealed and replaced by Supreme Decree No. 024-2016-EM and its amendments enacted pursuant to
Supreme Decree No. 029-2016-EM, Supreme Decree No. 029-2016-EM, Supreme Decree No. 023-2017-EM and
Supreme Decree No. 034-2023-EM.

          The main principle of this law is that the employer assumes the economic, legal and any other type of liability
arising from accidents or diseases suffered by the employee while working and guarantees the employee’s health and
safety in connection with the employee’s work. This legislation entitles labor inspectors to inspect commercial
facilities and, under certain circumstances, suspend operations. According to such laws and regulations, our main
obligations in connection with occupational safety and health rules are: (i) to establish a safety and health committee
which shall comprise the same number of employees and employer representatives and shall approve (A) an internal
occupational safety and health code, (B) an occupational safety and health annual program, and (C) an occupational
safety and health risk map, (ii) to implement and maintain a safety and health management system and its registries
and related documentation updated, (iii) to deliver a copy of the internal occupational safety and health code to its
employees, (iv) to supervise the employees’ fulfillment of the internal occupational safety and health code, (v) to
perform medical examinations prior, during and at the end of the employee’s labor relationship with us, (vi) to provide
employees the adequate protective equipment, (vii) to inform the labor authority regarding any deterioration in an
employee’s health, and (viii) to ensure the same safety and health standards apply to all members of our labor force
regardless if the employee is directly employed or through an outsourcing company.

          Emergency Decree No. 044-2019 amended Law No. 28806, General Labor Inspection Law and the Criminal
Code to establish measures to strengthen the protection of the health and lives of workers in Peru, by amending Law
No. 28806, the General Labor Inspection Law and the Criminal Code. This law included a new provision in the
criminal code, which now establishes that a person who intentionally breaches safety and health provisions and is
deemed to seriously jeopardize the life, health or physical integrity of such person’s employees may be held criminally
liable for such behavior and subject to mandatory sentencing of no less than one and no more than four years. If an
employee or third-party dies or is severely injured because of willful non-compliance with occupational health and
safety laws, such criminal offense would be punishable with mandatory imprisonment of no less than four and no
more than eight years. These punishments would be applied to the legal representative of the employer.

         The safety and health of our employees is our highest priority. Although we believe that we follow all safety
and health regulations in all material respects, we have implemented adequate safety measures and work continuously
to improve our occupational health and safety training and performance. We regularly monitor occupational health
and safety performance and compliance through safety training programs, review and analysis of audit reports,
accident reports, and other routine safety measures at our operating mines.

          Under Peruvian law, reportable injuries include accidental injuries resulting in lost-time, fatal accidents,
accidents that require medical treatment or restricted work, and hazardous incidents. Injuries involving first-aid only
are not reportable as they are considered minor accidents. During 2023 we experienced 48 reportable injuries,
including no fatal injuries, compared to 82 reportable injuries, including no fatal injuries in 2022. During 2024, we
experienced a total of 58 reportable injuries, including 1 regrettable fatal injury for the first time in the last 3 years.
During the nine-month period ended September 30, 2025, we experienced a total of 53 reportable injuries, with no
fatal injuries.

Labor Regulations

         Peruvian legislation allows the hiring of employees through: (i) a fixed-term contract, (ii) an indefinite-term
contract; or (iii) a part-time employment contract. The minimum wage established in Peru as of the date of this offering
memorandum is S/1,130.00 per month (US$330 approximately). Peruvian labor legislation establishes a maximum
working day of 8 hours a day or 48 hours a week for employees over 18 years of age. Likewise, the application of
cumulative or atypical days is allowed, as long as the average time worked is within the indicated maximum. Atypical
or cumulative days comprise a cycle in which workdays are accumulated in a continuous work block and rest days are
accumulated in another continuous block.

         In the case of overtime work, employers must pay at least an additional 25% and an additional 35% over the
regular hourly wage for the first two hours and for any additional hours, respectively. What is indicated applies to
both ordinary days and atypical or cumulative days.

Outsourcing

          According to Law No. 29245, complemented by Legislative Decree No. 1038 and the regulations enacted
thereunder, outsourcing is a form of business organization under which a company (main company) delegates part of
its main activities to one or more outsourcing companies. A “main activity” is an activity that, if not performed, would
immediately affect and/or interrupt the operations of a company.

          Under Peruvian law, companies may outsource their main activities provided that the following conditions
are met: (i) the outsourcing company must provide services at its own cost and risk, (ii) the outsourcing company must
have its own financial, technical or material resources, (iii) the outsourcing company must be responsible for the
results of its activities, and (iv) the employees of the outsourcing company must be under its exclusive subordination.
Failure to comply with any of the foregoing conditions renders the recognition of the employees as directly employed
by the main company, and the latter liable for all employment benefits as if the employees had been directly employed
by the main company.

           The following elements characterize outsourcing activities: (i) the outsourcing company has more than one
client, (ii) the outsourcing company has its own equipment and capital investment, and (iii) the compensation paid to
the outsourcing company is calculated based on the services rendered by the company (not based on the salaries of
the personnel assigned to the service).

         Pursuant to regulations governing outsourcing relationships, the main company is jointly responsible for the
payment of the main company employee’s remunerations, labor benefits and social security contributions accrued
during the term of the outsourcing relationship. Rights and benefits as a consequence of collective bargaining, labor
agreements or those unilaterally set forth by the employer are excluded. The main company’s joint responsibility
applies for up to one year after the conclusion of the term of the outsourcing relationship.

Electricity Regulatory Framework

        We hold a number of electricity concessions granted by MINEM or regional governments in order to conduct
our power generation and transmission activities. As a result, we are subject to the following regulatory framework.

         The Electricity Concessions Law, published in the Official Gazette, El Peruano, on November 19, 1992, is
the primary law governing electricity activities in Peru. The regulations to this law were enacted by means of Supreme
Decree No. 009-93-EM published in the Official Gazette, El Peruano, on February 25, 1993.

         On July 23, 2006, the Peruvian government enacted the Law to Secure the Efficient Development of Power
Generation (Ley para Asegurar el Desarrollo Eficiente de la Generación Eléctrica), approved by Law No. 28832,
which approved important modifications to the regulatory framework set forth in the Electricity Concessions Law.
Both laws have been supplemented by several regulations regarding quality conditions for energy provision, tariff
calculation, environmental, water use, wastewater disposal, cultural heritage protection, and other applicable permits
required to develop electricity activities. In 2025, Law No. 28832 was amended by Law No. 32249. The modifications
included in this law will allow the separate sale of capacity and energy and would modify, among other aspects, the
mechanism of public tenders applicable to distribution companies for the acquisition of capacity and energy. The



                                                          114

entry into force of the modifications to Law No. 28832 set forth in Law No. 32249 is subject to the approval of the
applicable regulations, which is still pending as of the date of this offering memorandum.

          According to the foregoing laws, the following electricity activities shall be carried out exclusively through
(i) a definitive concession, in the case of hydroelectric plants and other type of plants that use renewable energy
resources with installed power capacity higher than 500 kW, power transmission activities that affect state-owned
property or require the imposition of easements, and power distribution with a demand of over 500 kW, or
(ii) authorizations in the case of thermoelectric power generation with an installed capacity that exceeds 500 kW. Both
concessions and authorizations are granted by MINEM or by regional governments (in case of plants with installed
power capacity greater than 500 kW and less than 10 MW).

         Also, in accordance with the Non-Regulated Users Rules (Reglamento de Usuarios Libres), approved by
Supreme Decree No. 022-2009-EM, users are qualified according to their degree of power consumption. Electricity
users that have power demands larger than 2.5 MW in each supply point per year are considered non-regulated users
and therefore have the right to choose their energy supplier. Electricity users whose maximum annual demand from
each supply point is greater than 0.2MW up to 2.5 MW have the right to choose their status as regulated or non-
regulated users. Users with a demand up to 0.2 MW are considered regulated clients.

          The Supervisory Agency of Investment in Energy and Mining (Organismo Supervisor de la Inversión en
Energía y Minería - OSINERGMIN) is an independent entity that has the power and responsibility to, among other
things: (i) supervise participants’ compliance with their concession agreements, legal obligations and regulations, as
well as with the technical rules relating to the generation, transmission, distribution and commercialization of power;
(ii) administer fines and penalties in case of violations of laws and regulations; (iii) handle claims by, between or
against consumers and/or the energy sector participants and (iv) promote competition, transparency and equity in the
energy market.

         The Peruvian government, through OSINERGMIN, regulates and supervises the tariff (Bus Bar Tariff) to be
charged by the electricity distributors that provide the energy distribution public service (regulated users). Distributors
are required to purchase their energy supply with generators and two different regimes may apply: (i) bilateral
agreements with generators, and (ii) contracts resulting from public tenders, called by distributors, in which the
contract price will be the one offered by each bidder, with the maximum price being the one set by OSINERGMIN
for each tender process. However, in the case of energy supply required by distributors for their energy demand from
non-regulated users, the electricity supply conditions shall be freely agreed with the generators.

         Generation companies may sell electricity to distribution companies and non-regulated users. In the latter
case, electricity prices (energy and power) are freely negotiable, but the tariffs and compensations for the use of the
transmission networks and distribution networks, if applicable, are subject to the regulations issued by
OSINERGMIN.

          According to articles 36 and 105 of the Electricity Concessions Law, the government is entitled to terminate
a definitive concession agreement in the case of certain events, including the following:

         •    If the concessionaire fails to communicate to the MINEM the registration of its concession agreement
              in public records within 20 business days from the date of registration.

         •    If the concessionaire breaches its works schedule unless it was a consequence of a force majeure event,
              qualified as such by the MINEM, or a new guaranteed works schedule is approved.

         •    If the concessionaire stops operating its facilities without cause for over 876 hours during a calendar
              year.

         •    If, the relevant generation or transmission concessionaire, after the imposition of fines, continues to
              operate its facilities without following the orders of the Economic Committee of the System (COES).

         •    If the MINEM unilaterally terminates the concession for reasons other than those expressly established
              in the Electricity Concessions Law.

Termination of a definitive concession is not automatic and requires the commencement of an administrative
proceeding by the MINEM, followed by the issuance of a ministerial resolution by the MINEM.

        According to article 69 of the regulations of the Electricity Concessions Law, the government is entitled to
revoke the authorizations for the development of electricity activities in the case of certain events, including the
following:

         •   For repeated violations related to the protection of the environment or of the nation’s cultural heritage
             that has been officially declared as such at the time of executing the works.

         •   If the owner of a generation plant that is part of an interconnected system, after the imposition of the
             corresponding sanctions, fails to operate its facilities in accordance with the coordination rules of the
             Economic Committee of the System (COES).

         •   If the owner fails to execute the works and installations within the time limits established in the approved
             schedule, except in cases of force majeure, fortuitous events, or duly substantiated and approved
             technical-economic reasons. Such technical-economic reasons may only be invoked once and shall be
             approved when they are beyond the control of the owner and/or its economic group and constitute a
             direct cause of the non-compliance.

          If the revocation of the authorization for the development of electricity activities compromises the public
electricity service, the requirements and procedures established for the termination of a definitive concession must
apply, insofar as they are relevant. Otherwise, a favorable report from the General Directorate of Electricity (DGE) of
the MINEM or the regional government should be enough to revoke the authorization.

        The revocation of the authorization for the development of electricity activities must be declared by the
corresponding resolution, which must also order the execution of any guarantees that remain in force.

          Holders of electricity concessions and authorizations must comply with several obligations, including the

billing net of value-added tax (18%). Such contribution shall be equal to the following percentages:

    •    OSINERGMIN:                0.41% for 2026, 0.38% for 2027 and 0.35% for 2028
    •    OEFA:                      0.12% for 2026, 0.11% for 2027 and 0.10% for 2028

Marco de los Organismos Reguladores de la Inversión Privada en los Servicios Públicos), approved by Law No.

Our Share Capital

        Our shares are divided in two classes: Class A shares and Class B shares. Class A shares are entitled to vote,
while Class B shares have no voting rights (except in exceptional cases) but are entitled to preferential rights in
connection with dividend distributions.

         Holders of Class A shares are entitled to one vote per share, with the exception of the election of the board
of directors, where each holder is entitled to one vote per share per nominee. Each holder’s votes may be cast for a
single nominee or distributed among the nominees at the holder’s discretion.

          Holders of Class B shares have a preferential right in connection with the distribution of dividends.
Accordingly, Class B holders are entitled to receive an additional 5% over the applicable dividend paid to Class A
holders. In addition, Class B holders are not entitled to attend shareholders meetings or to exercise voting rights
therein, except in the following cases:

•          when a shareholders meeting discusses any of the following matters: (i) capital reduction, (ii) merger, spin-
           off, transformation, dissolution or liquidation, (iii) changes on our domicile to any country other than Peru,
           (iv) bylaws’ amendments related to our principal corporate purpose or the duration of our existence;

                                                                      120

•        when we fail to comply with the preferential cash dividend applicable to holders of Class B shares and only
         while such non-compliance continues, or when we intend to modify or exclude any right to which the Class
         B holders are entitled to; and

•        when a suspension or exclusion of our shares from the Lima Stock Exchange occurs and is attributable to us
         and only while such situation continues.

        In any of the foregoing cases, holders of Class B shares are entitled to attend the relevant shareholders
meeting and to exercise one vote per share. In these cases, all Class B shares are counted for quorum purposes.

           Shareholders’ meetings consist of annual mandatory meetings or general meetings. The annual mandatory
meeting has to take place within the first 90 days of each year, and has to treat the following matters: (i) approval or
disapproval of the management, accounts and balance sheet of the foregoing year; (ii) decide on the allocation of
profits; (iii) appoint the members of the board and determine their compensation; (iv) appoint, or delegate on the board
of directors the appointment of, the external auditors; and (v) resolve on other aspects to which it is entitled to by
virtue of the bylaws and/or applicable laws.

          The general meetings have to treat following matters: (i) issuance of bonds or other debt instruments; (ii)
amendments and interpretation of the bylaws; (iii) capital increases or reductions; (iv) transfer of all or of a substantial
part of our assets; (v) merger, spin-off, transformation, reorganization, dissolution and liquidation; (vi) removal of the
members of the board of directors and appointment of new members; (vii) order special investigations and audits; and
(viii) cases for which the bylaws or the law provide for its intervention or the corporate interest requires. In order to
adopt the agreements mentioned in (i) through (v), the required quorum and majorities are higher than those needed
for the adoption of other resolutions.

RELATED PARTY TRANSACTIONS

         In the ordinary course of business, we engage in a variety of transactions with subsidiaries, affiliates and
related parties, including loan agreements and agreements relating to the sale of our products, sale of goods,
management services, ore processing services, mineral and concentrate storage services and provision of labor.

         Peruvian law imposes certain restrictions and limitations on transactions with related parties. For instance,
from a tax standpoint, related-party transactions are subject to Peruvian transfer pricing rules. Under those rules, if the
value agreed to by the parties differs from the market value determined under the applicable transfer pricing rules, the
tax consequences of the transaction may be determined by reference to the price or consideration that would have been
agreed to by independent parties in comparable transactions under the same or similar circumstances, or through any
other transfer pricing method permitted under Peruvian law.

         Similarly, as a company with at least one class of securities registered in the Public Registry of the Securities
Market (Registro Público del Mercado de Valores) of the SMV, we are subject to Article 51(c) of the Peruvian
Securities Market Law and its regulations approved by SMV Resolution N° 029-2018-SMV/01, as amended.
Accordingly, we are required to comply with, among others, the following rules:

•        Transactions involving at least 5% of the issuer’s assets which involve individuals or legal entities related to
         its directors, managers or shareholders that directly or indirectly represent more than 10% of the issuer’s
         share capital require the prior approval of the board of directors, without the participation of the director that
         has the relevant relationship (if any); and

•        Transactions in which the issuer’s controlling shareholder also controls the legal entity acting as counterparty
         to the relevant act or agreement which was subject to prior board approval must have their terms reviewed
         by an entity external to the issuer. Such external entity may be an audit firm or any other legal entity
         determined by the SMV through general regulations, and such external entity must, among other
         requirements, not be related to the parties involved in the transaction or to their directors, managers or
         shareholders holding at least 10% of their share capital.

        Such regulations also provide that if it is not possible for a company’s board of directors to decide on the
execution of the agreement, it must be approved by such company’s general shareholders’ meeting.

           Once the commencement of an insolvency procedure of a Peruvian company, such as the Company and
 the Subsidiary Guarantors, is made public, two main consequences are immediately triggered (a) the automatic
 stay of enforcement of all of the debtor’s obligations (whether monetary or non-monetary); and (b) the protection
 of the debtor’s estate (assets) by means of the suspension of all judicial or extra-judicial collection and foreclosure
 proceedings filed by any creditor and, in general, the suspension of all acts intended to create or enforce any lien,
 security or mortgage against the property of the debtor, except those that have been transferred to a trust (like the
 Equity Interests Trust Agreement, the Existing Trusts and the New Cash Flows Trust). The automatic stay will
 prevent the Peruvian Collateral Agent from pursuing enforcement of the mortgages created under the Mortgages
 over Production Units Agreement and the Mortgages over Real Property Agreements. The automatic stay of
 enforcement of all of the debtor’s obligations does not prevent creditors from enforcing their rights against third
 parties which have granted corporate or asset-based guarantees, who will assume the contractual position of the
 original debtor. Moreover, under the Peruvian Bankruptcy Law, once the debtor files for insolvency, or is given
 notice of an involuntary filing, all actions taken by management during the previous year (clawback period) and
 from that date on and until the date the creditors ratify or replace management (avoidance period) may be under
 specific judicial scrutiny. The clawback period covers all actions or transactions taken by management during the
 previous year, whether for consideration or not, that have a negative effect on the net worth of the company and
 are not in the ordinary course of business (all requirements must be met). The avoidance period covers actions or
 transactions specifically detailed under the Peruvian Bankruptcy Law.
          The Peruvian Bankruptcy Law does not recognize nor regulate group insolvency. It regulates the
 insolvency proceedings on a company-by-company basis and does not include any regulation relating to
 proceedings covering more than one legal entity or entitling creditors of insolvent companies or the companies
 themselves to include other entities of the same corporate group in the same insolvency proceeding. Consequently,
 the insolvency proceeding cannot be used to liquidate or reorganize a corporate group on a combined basis. There
 are no special proceedings or impediments or protections applicable to foreign creditors. Also, in Peru foreign
 creditors are entitled to the same rights and benefits as Peruvian creditors in connection with an insolvency
 proceeding. Finally, in the event of an insolvency proceeding, if a debtor is domiciled in Peru it will be subject to

 Intelectual – INDECOPI.

Change of Control Triggering Event
         Upon the occurrence of a Change of Control Triggering Event, each Holder will have the right to require that
the Company purchase all or a portion of such Holder’s Notes (in integral multiples of US$1,000; provided that the
remaining principal amount of such Holder’s Note will not be less than US$2,000) of the Holder’s Notes at a purchase
price equal to 101% of the principal amount thereof, plus any accrued and unpaid interest thereon to but excluding the
purchase date (the “Change of Control Payment”).
         Within thirty (30) days following the date upon which the Change of Control Triggering Event occurs, the
Company must send a notice to each Holder, with a copy to the Trustee, offering to purchase the Notes as described
above (a “Change of Control Offer”) as described in “—Notices” below. The Change of Control Offer will state,
among other things, the purchase date, which must be at least ten (10) but not more than sixty (60) days from the date
the notice is given, other than as may be required by law (the “Change of Control Payment Date”). The Change of
Control Offer may, at the Company’s discretion, be subject to the consummation of the transactions triggering the
Change of Control Triggering Event as a condition precedent.
         On the Business Day immediately preceding the Change of Control Payment Date, the Company will, to the
extent lawful, deposit with the paying agent funds in an amount equal to the Change of Control Payment, in respect
of all Notes or portions thereof so tendered.
           On the Change of Control Payment Date, as applicable, the Company will, to the extent lawful:
     (1)        accept for payment all Notes or portions thereof properly tendered and not withdrawn; and
     (2)        deliver or cause to be delivered to the Trustee the Notes so accepted together with an Officer’s
                Certificate stating the aggregate principal amount of Notes or portions thereof being purchased by the
                Company.
         If only a portion of a Note is purchased pursuant to a Change of Control Offer, as applicable, a new Note in
an authorized principal amount equal to the portion thereof not purchased will be issued in the name of the Holder
thereof upon cancellation of the original Note (or appropriate adjustments to the amount and beneficial interests in a
Global Note will be made, as appropriate). Notes (or portions thereof) purchased pursuant to a Change of Control
Offer, as applicable, will be cancelled and cannot be reissued.
          The Company will comply with the requirements of Rule 14e-1 under the Exchange Act and any other
securities laws and regulations to the extent any such rule, laws and regulations are applicable in connection with the
purchase of Notes in connection with a Change of Control Offer, as applicable. To the extent that the provisions of
any applicable securities laws or regulations conflict with the Change of Control Triggering Event provisions of the
Indenture, the Company will comply with such securities laws and regulations and will not be deemed to have
breached its obligations under the Indenture by doing so.
